title: Waste after the bin: what rots, what stays, and where it all goes

summary.text: Since 1950, people have made more than 8 billion tonnes of plastic. In 2017 scientists worked out where it went. About four fifths still lies in dumps, on land or in the sea. Waste does not vanish when the truck takes it. Organic waste, such as peels and paper, can be eaten by decomposers. Inorganic waste, such as glass and metal, cannot, and neither can plastic. Your child tests why plastics must be sorted kind by kind, and peels a carton into its layers. They weigh the family's waste for seven days. They also learn what dumping and burning do to soil, water and air.
summary.art: A cut-away picture of a city waste dump: a truck tipping waste at the top, layers of old waste below, and a thin dark stream of dirty water seeping down towards a well.

intro.hook: The waste truck comes every morning, and the bin is empty again. Where is that waste tonight? Where will it be when you are fifty years old?
intro.text: People say they throw waste 'away'. But every peel, bottle and packet goes to a real place and stays made of the same atoms. Some of it rots within weeks. Some of it can be melted and made into new things. Some of it lies in a dump for hundreds of years, or is burnt and goes into the air. In this unit you find out which waste does which, and why. You also find out what your own family's waste is made of.
intro.art: A girl at a balcony watching a waste truck drive off down a street, with a dotted line running from the truck to a far grey hill of waste on the horizon.

outcomes: By the end I can sort waste into organic and inorganic, and say why decomposers can eat only one kind.
By the end I can say where the matter goes when waste is composted, dumped, buried or burnt.
By the end I can explain how dumped and burnt waste harms soil, water, air, other animals and people.
By the end I can use my Float Tank Test results to explain why plastics must be sorted.
By the end I can find the materials in a packet, and say why joined materials are hard to recycle.
By the end I can name the hazardous waste and e-waste in my home and say where each goes.
By the end I can weigh my family's waste for a week, chart it and plan to make less.
By the end I can argue with evidence about city waste, and name one thing nobody knows yet.

terms.meaning: Anything a person decides they no longer want and throws out. The same thing can be waste to one person and useful to another.
terms.example: An old newspaper is waste in your home. The kabadiwala pays for it, because a paper mill can use it.
terms.art: A stack of old newspapers by a door, with a scrap dealer weighing a bundle on a hand balance.

terms.meaning: Waste that came from living beings, such as plants and animals. Decomposers can eat it, so it rots.
terms.example: Vegetable peels, leftover rice, dry leaves, paper, cotton cloth and wood are organic waste.
terms.art: A heap of peels, a dry leaf, a sheet of newspaper and a cotton rag grouped together on a table.

terms.meaning: Waste that did not come from living beings. It is made from rocks, sand and metal ores, and decomposers cannot eat it.
terms.example: Glass bottles, steel tins, aluminium foil and broken tiles are inorganic waste. Waste rules also put plastic in this group.
terms.art: A glass bottle, a steel tin, a ball of foil and a broken tile grouped together on a table.

terms.meaning: Able to be broken down by decomposers into soil, water and gases.
terms.example: A banana leaf plate is biodegradable. In a compost pot, decomposers finish eating one in a few weeks.
terms.art: A banana leaf half turned to dark crumbly compost, with tiny threads of fungus on it.

terms.meaning: Not able to be broken down by decomposers, or broken down so slowly that it lasts for lifetimes.
terms.example: A plastic carry bag is non-biodegradable. Sunlight cracks it into small pieces, but the pieces stay plastic.
terms.art: A faded, cracked plastic carry bag lying half buried in soil.

terms.meaning: A living being who feeds on dead plants, dead animals and droppings, and turns them into soil and gases. Most decomposers are fungi and bacteria.
terms.example: The white threads in a compost pot are fungi. They are eating the peels.
terms.art: A close view of white fungal threads spreading over a piece of orange peel.

terms.meaning: Keeping different kinds of waste apart from the moment they are thrown. India's waste rules ask every home to keep three kinds apart.
terms.example: A home with a wet bin, a dry bag and a small box for hazardous waste is segregating.
terms.art: Three containers in a kitchen corner: a green bin, a blue bag and a small red box with a lid.

terms.meaning: Dark, crumbly matter that is left when decomposers have eaten organic waste with plenty of air. It feeds plants.
terms.example: A pot of peels mixed with dry leaves becomes compost in about two months.
terms.art: Two hands in gloves holding dark, crumbly compost over a clay pot.

terms.meaning: A gas with no colour and no smell that burns. Some microbes make it when they break down organic waste where there is no air.
terms.example: Deep inside a dump there is no air. The food waste there gives off methane, which can catch fire.
terms.art: A cut-away of a waste heap with bubbles of gas rising from the dark, packed bottom layer.

terms.meaning: A mix of methane and carbon dioxide that people make on purpose and burn as fuel. Microbes make it from wet waste in a closed tank with no air.
terms.example: A biogas plant in a village turns cow dung and kitchen waste into gas for cooking.
terms.art: A round biogas tank beside a cowshed, with a pipe leading to a blue flame on a kitchen stove.

terms.meaning: A piece of land where mixed waste is tipped and left in the open. Nothing lies under the waste and nothing covers it.
terms.example: Ghazipur in Delhi and Deonar in Mumbai are open dumps that have grown into hills.
terms.art: A grey hill of mixed waste with kites circling above it and smoke rising from one side.

terms.meaning: A place built for burying waste safely. It has a liner underneath, pipes to take out dirty water and gas, and a cover of soil.
terms.example: In a well-built landfill, each day's waste is pressed down and covered with soil.
terms.art: A cut-away of an engineered landfill showing a clay and plastic liner, pipes at the bottom, layers of waste and a soil cover.

terms.meaning: The dirty liquid that drains out of a heap of waste. Rainwater soaks through the waste and carries dissolved matter with it.
terms.example: The dark liquid at the bottom of a kitchen bin is leachate. Under a dump, it can reach the groundwater.
terms.art: A dark trickle of liquid running out from the bottom of a waste heap into the soil.

terms.meaning: Burning waste in a closed furnace at very high heat. Some plants use the heat to make electricity.
terms.example: A waste-to-energy plant incinerates mixed waste. It still leaves ash, and it sends gases up its chimney.
terms.art: A factory building with a tall chimney, a truck tipping waste into a pit and a heap of grey ash at the back.

terms.meaning: Breaking a used thing down into its material, and making new things from that material.
terms.example: Old glass bottles are crushed, melted and blown into new bottles.
terms.art: A row of pictures: a used glass bottle, crushed glass, glowing melted glass and a new bottle.

terms.meaning: Recycling a material into something of lower quality, which often cannot be recycled again.
terms.example: Clear drink bottles are often made into polyester fibre for cloth. That cloth is not made back into bottles.
terms.art: A clear plastic bottle with an arrow to a fleece jacket, and a crossed-out arrow leading back to the bottle.

terms.meaning: The number from 1 to 7 inside a small triangle on a plastic thing. It tells which kind of plastic the thing is made of.
terms.example: A drink bottle has a 1 on its base. A takeaway box often has a 5.
terms.art: The base of a plastic bottle seen close up, with a small triangle of arrows and the number 1 inside.

terms.meaning: How much matter is packed into each bit of space. A material denser than water sinks in water, and a less dense one floats.
terms.example: A piece of drink bottle is denser than water and sinks. A piece of its cap is less dense and floats.
terms.art: A glass bowl of water with one clear plastic piece on the bottom and one blue piece floating on top.

terms.meaning: A packet made of thin layers of different materials stuck together, such as plastic, metal and paper.
terms.example: A chips packet is plastic film with a very thin coat of aluminium. A juice carton is paper, plastic and foil.
terms.art: A juice carton wall peeled apart at one corner into a clear film, a paper layer and a silver layer.

terms.meaning: Waste that can poison, burn or cut living beings, even in small amounts. It must be kept apart from other waste.
terms.example: Used batteries, old medicines, tube lights, paint tins and insect spray cans are hazardous waste.
terms.art: A small box holding a battery, a strip of tablets, a tube light end and a spray can, with a warning sign on the lid.

terms.meaning: Electrical and electronic things that are thrown out. E-waste holds useful metals and also harmful ones.
terms.example: An old phone, a dead charger and a broken remote are e-waste. They go to an e-waste collector, not the dry bin.
terms.art: A broken phone, a tangled charger and a remote control in a cardboard box marked for collection.

terms.meaning: A piece of plastic smaller than 5 millimetres. Big plastic things crack into microplastics, which do not rot.
terms.example: A thermocol plate rubbed between the hands breaks into tiny white beads. Each bead is still plastic.
terms.art: A fingertip with a few tiny coloured plastic specks on it, beside a ruler showing millimetres.

terms.meaning: A list of what to do about waste, with the best choice first: refuse and reduce, reuse, recycle, recover, and last of all dispose.
terms.example: Carrying a steel bottle is reducing. It is better than recycling a plastic bottle, because no waste is made.
terms.art: An upside-down triangle in five bands, the widest at the top labelled 'reduce' and the smallest at the bottom labelled 'dispose'.

explanations.definition: Organic waste came from living beings, and decomposers can break it down. Inorganic waste came from rocks, sand and metal ores, and decomposers cannot break it down.
explanations.description: Fungi and bacteria have fed on dead plants and animals for hundreds of millions of years. They have enzymes, which are tiny tools that cut food into pieces small enough to take in. So anything built by a living being has someone who can eat it. That is why peels, paper, cotton, wood and leather rot. Glass is melted sand, and metals come from ores dug out of rock. No decomposer feeds on them, so they do not rot. Organic does not mean wet. Paper and cotton are dry, but they are organic. Plastic is harder to place. It is made from oil, and oil formed from tiny sea beings who died millions of years ago. But factories join its atoms into very long chains that almost no decomposer can cut. So waste rules put plastic with inorganic waste.
examples: Organic waste includes vegetable peels, leftover food, dry leaves, flowers, paper, cardboard, cotton, jute, wood and hair.
Inorganic waste includes glass bottles, steel tins, aluminium foil, broken cups and broken tiles.
Plastic includes milk packets, bottles, wrappers and thermocol. It is made from ancient living beings, but it is treated as inorganic waste because it does not rot.
In Once Alive or Never Alive, an eggshell and a coconut shell are organic, though they rot slowly.
explanations.art: Two groups of waste on a table, one with peels, paper, cotton and a leaf, the other with glass, steel and foil, and a plastic bottle standing on the line between them.

explanations.concept: What decomposers do to organic waste, with air and without air
explanations.definition: With plenty of air, decomposers turn organic waste into compost, carbon dioxide, water and heat. Without air, other microbes turn it into methane, carbon dioxide and strong-smelling gases.
explanations.description: Decomposers who use air work fast, and their heap smells like damp earth. This is composting. A good part of the mass of the peels leaves as carbon dioxide and water vapour. The rest stays as dark compost. Deep inside a packed dump, the air is soon used up. A different set of microbes takes over there. They work slowly and give off methane. Methane burns, so it can start fires inside a dump. Methane also traps heat in the air. Over a hundred years, methane warms the Earth about 28 times as much as the same mass of carbon dioxide. A biogas plant uses the same microbes on purpose. It keeps wet waste in a closed tank, collects the methane and burns it as fuel. The slurry that is left goes to fields as manure.
examples: A balcony compost pot with dry leaves mixed in has air, and makes compost in about two months.
Food waste buried under tonnes of other waste has no air, and makes methane for many years.
Many homes in Indian villages cook on biogas made from cow dung in a tank beside the house.
Indore sends wet waste to a large plant that makes gas for city buses.
explanations.art: A split picture: on the left an airy compost heap with steam rising and a label 'with air', on the right a sealed tank with a pipe carrying gas to a flame and a label 'without air'.

explanations.concept: Open dumps and landfills: what happens under the heap
explanations.definition: An open dump is waste tipped on bare land. A landfill is built to hold waste. It has a liner below, pipes for dirty water and gas, and a cover of soil.
explanations.description: Rain falls on a dump and soaks down through the waste. On the way it picks up rotting matter, salts, and metals from batteries and paints. The dark liquid that drains out is called leachate. Under an open dump, leachate seeps into the soil and can reach the groundwater that wells and borewells draw from. Inside the heap, buried food waste makes methane, and the heap can smoulder for weeks. A heap that grows too tall and steep can also slide. A well-built landfill is designed to stop each of these. A layer of pressed clay and a thick plastic sheet line the bottom. Pipes carry the leachate to a treatment tank. Other pipes collect the methane. Each day's waste is covered with soil. Even so, a landfill only stores the waste. Someone must look after it for many years after it is full.
examples: At Ghazipur in Delhi, the dump grew into a hill some 50 to 65 metres high, and reports differ. In 2017 a part of it slid down and killed two people.
In 2016 the Deonar dump in Mumbai burned for days, and the smoke could be seen in pictures from space.
In A Dump That Does Not Leak, you build a small lined dump and test whether it leaks.
explanations.art: A cut-away comparing two heaps: an open dump with dark liquid seeping into a well, and a lined landfill with pipes carrying the liquid to a tank.

explanations.definition: When waste burns, its atoms join with oxygen and leave as gases and smoke. A little ash stays behind. No atom is destroyed.
explanations.description: A sheet of paper weighs far more than the ash it leaves. The missing matter did not vanish. Most of it went into the air as carbon dioxide and water vapour, with some smoke. Smoke is made of tiny solid specks that reach deep into the lungs. Burning plastic sends out more than smoke. Some plastics hold chlorine, and when they burn in an open fire they make poisons called dioxins. So a fire moves waste from the ground into the air that everyone breathes. Antoine Lavoisier, a French chemist, showed in the 1780s that matter is never lost in burning. He weighed everything before and after, in sealed glass vessels. Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier worked with him, kept the records and drew the equipment.
examples: A heap of dry leaves burnt on the street becomes smoke, gases and a handful of ash.
Dump fires are often started by methane, and can burn for days.
In Where Did the Peel Go, you draw what leaves a burning peel and where it ends up.
explanations.art: A burning heap of mixed waste with arrows showing grey smoke and unseen gases rising, and a small pile of ash left on the ground.

explanations.concept: Plastic is many materials: the number in the triangle
explanations.definition: 'Plastic' is a name for many different materials. The resin code is a number from 1 to 7 in a small triangle. It tells which kind a thing is made of.
explanations.description: Every plastic is made of very long chain molecules, but the chains differ. In a drink bottle, marked 1, the chains hold carbon, hydrogen and oxygen atoms and pack closely. That plastic is denser than water, so a piece of it sinks. In a bottle cap or a milk packet, the chains hold only carbon and hydrogen, like candle wax. Those plastics are less dense than water, so they float. Different plastics also melt at different temperatures and do not mix well when melted. A batch with two kinds in it makes a weak, cloudy plastic. So a recycling factory wants one kind at a time. The triangle on a thing only names the kind. It is not a promise that the thing will be recycled.
examples: Code 1 is PET. It is used for water and soft drink bottles, and it sinks in water.
Code 2 is HDPE. It is used for shampoo bottles and many bottle caps, and it floats.
Code 3 is PVC. It is used for pipes and some shrink labels, and it sinks.
Code 4 is LDPE. It is used for milk packets and carry bags, and it floats.
Code 5 is PP. It is used for takeaway boxes, many caps and straws, and it floats.
Code 6 is PS. It is used for some disposable cups and spoons, and for thermocol. Solid pieces sink slowly in plain water, and float in salty water.
Code 7 is used for all other plastics, and for mixtures of plastics.
explanations.art: Seven small plastic things in a row, each with its triangle and number drawn large beside it: a drink bottle, a shampoo bottle, a pipe, a milk packet, a takeaway box, a disposable cup and a mixed-plastic toy.

explanations.concept: Recycling, downcycling and what is never recycled
explanations.definition: Recycling makes new things from the material of old ones. How many times a material can be recycled depends on the material.
explanations.description: Glass and metals can be melted and remade again and again. The new thing is as good as the old. Making a can from old aluminium takes about one twentieth of the energy of making it from ore. Paper is different. Each time it is pulped, its fibres get shorter, so paper can be recycled only a few times, often about four to seven. Plastic is usually downcycled. A clear bottle becomes fibre for cloth or filling, and that product is not recycled again. Multi-layer packets are the hardest. Their layers of plastic, metal and paper are stuck together and cannot be pulled apart cheaply. Scientists counted all the plastic made up to 2015. Only about 9 kilograms in every 100 had been recycled. About 12 had been burnt. About 79 were in dumps and landfills, or loose in the environment.
examples: An aluminium can sold as scrap can be back in a shop as a new can within months.
A newspaper becomes an egg tray or a cardboard box.
A chips packet is light and keeps food crisp, but almost no factory can recycle it.
In Scrunch and Peel, you find three materials in one juice carton.
explanations.art: Three loops side by side: a tight closed loop for a glass bottle, a spiral that gets smaller for paper, and a single arrow from a plastic bottle to a jacket that ends in a bin.

explanations.concept: How waste harms soil, water, air and living beings
explanations.definition: Waste harms when it reaches a place where it blocks, poisons or is eaten. The harm depends on what the waste is made of and where it ends up.
explanations.description: On land, plastic sheets in the soil stop water soaking in and roots spreading. Cows, dogs and goats who feed at open bins swallow plastic bags with the food inside them. The bags stay in a cow's stomach, and she can starve with a full belly. In water, plastic bags block drains, and streets flood. Organic waste harms water too. When food waste is tipped into a pond, microbes multiply to eat it. They use up the oxygen dissolved in the water, and fish die. Leachate from dumps carries salts and metals into wells. In the air, burning waste adds smoke and poisons, and dumps add methane. In the sea, sunlight and waves crack plastic into microplastics. Fish, birds and turtles swallow them. Microplastics have now been found in salt, in drinking water and in human blood.
examples: In July 2005, very heavy rain flooded Mumbai. Drains choked with plastic bags made it worse, and the state then banned the thinnest bags.
Vets in India have removed many kilograms of plastic bags from the stomachs of street cows.
People who live beside dumps breathe the smoke and often drink the water from nearby wells.
explanations.art: Four small scenes: a cow eating from a plastic bag at a bin, a flooded street with bags over a drain, fish gasping at the surface of a green pond, and smoke from a dump drifting over houses.

explanations.concept: Hazardous waste and e-waste at home
explanations.definition: Hazardous waste can poison, burn or cut, even in small amounts. E-waste is any thrown-out thing that used electricity. Both are kept apart from wet and dry waste.
explanations.description: A used battery holds metals such as lead, cadmium or lithium. In a dump its case rusts open, and the metals leak into the leachate. A crushed lithium battery can also catch fire in a waste truck. Tube lights and CFL bulbs hold a little mercury, which is set free when they break. Old medicines, paint, insect sprays and strong cleaners are poisons. Broken glass, blades and needles cut the hands of the people who sort waste. So these go in a separate, closed box, and blades and glass are wrapped in thick paper and marked. Used sanitary pads and nappies are wrapped in paper too. E-waste is a special case. An old phone holds lead and also copper, silver and gold. A tonne of old phones holds many times more gold than a tonne of gold ore. So e-waste goes to an authorised e-waste collector, who can recover the metals safely.
examples: Hazardous waste includes batteries, tube lights, CFL bulbs, old medicines, paint tins, insect spray cans, blades and broken thermometers.
E-waste includes phones, chargers, earphones, remotes, toys with circuits and old computers.
India makes millions of tonnes of e-waste every year, the third most of any country.
explanations.art: A small red box with a lid on a shelf, holding batteries, a strip of tablets and a wrapped bundle marked 'glass', and beside it a cardboard box with an old phone and a charger.

explanations.concept: The waste hierarchy and India's waste rules
explanations.definition: The waste hierarchy puts the choices about waste in order. Refuse and reduce come first, then reuse, then recycle, then recover, and dispose comes last.
explanations.description: The order follows one idea. The earlier the step, the less matter has to be moved, melted or stored. Refusing a carry bag makes no waste at all. Reusing a jar needs only washing. Recycling needs collecting, sorting and melting. Recovering means getting something back from what cannot be recycled, such as compost or biogas from wet waste. Disposing in a landfill gets nothing back. India's Solid Waste Management Rules of 2016 follow this order. They ask every home to keep three kinds of waste apart: wet waste, dry waste and domestic hazardous waste. Flats and offices that make a lot of waste must compost their own wet waste. Other rules make the companies that sell things in plastic packets pay to collect that plastic back. In 2022 India also banned some plastic things that are used once, such as plastic straws and thermocol plates.
examples: To refuse and reduce, carry a cloth bag and a steel bottle, and buy loose vegetables.
To reuse, keep glass jars for dal, and pass on outgrown clothes.
To recycle, sell paper, metal, glass and clean plastic to the kabadiwala.
To recover, compost the wet waste, or send it to a biogas plant.
To dispose, send only what is left to a landfill.
explanations.art: An upside-down triangle in five coloured bands labelled from the top: refuse and reduce, reuse, recycle, recover, dispose.

explanations.definition: A city handles its waste well when three things happen. Homes segregate the waste. Wet waste is composted or made into gas nearby. Dry waste is sorted and sold.
explanations.description: Indore in Madhya Pradesh once had bins overflowing on its streets. From 2016 the city removed the street bins and sent a truck to every door each day. The truck has separate boxes, so wet and dry waste never mix. Wet waste goes to compost plants and to a large biogas plant. Dry waste goes to sorting centres. Indore was ranked India's cleanest city in the national survey every year from 2017, for at least seven years in a row. Alappuzha in Kerala took another path. In 2012 the people of the village beside its dump blocked the trucks, because the dump was spoiling their water. The town then asked each home and each street to compost its own wet waste. People used pipes, pots and shared bins. Both cities began with the same step, which was keeping wet and dry waste apart at home.
examples: In Indore, one truck comes to every door, with separate boxes for each kind of waste.
In Alappuzha, there are compost bins in homes and at street corners, and a small biogas plant where there is room.
In The Last Landfill, you run a city and choose what to build first.
explanations.art: A waste truck with three separate coloured boxes stopping at a doorway, with a woman tipping a green bin into the green box.

explanations.concept: The people who sort our waste
explanations.definition: Waste pickers and sorters collect what others throw out, sort it by material and sell it to recyclers. Most of India's recycling begins with their hands.
explanations.description: Estimates say that somewhere between one and a half and four million people in India earn their living from waste. Many of them are women. They walk the streets and the dumps and pick out paper, metal, glass and plastic. Skilled sorters can tell one plastic from another by its sound when squeezed, its feel and the way it bends. This work saves cities a great deal of money and landfill space. But the work is risky. Mixed waste hides broken glass, blades, needles and rotting food. In Pune, waste pickers own a cooperative called SWaCH, which has worked with the city since 2008. Its members collect segregated waste from homes for a fee, with gloves, carts and identity cards. When a home keeps its waste clean and separate, the person who sorts it is safer and earns more.
examples: A milk packet that is rinsed and dried can be sold. A packet full of sour milk is thrown on the dump.
Broken glass wrapped in newspaper and marked 'glass' does not cut anyone's hand.
In The Scrap Price Chart, you find out what each material earns for the person who collects it.
explanations.art: A woman in gloves and an apron at a sorting table, holding a plastic bottle up to her ear and squeezing it, with sacks of sorted plastic behind her.

explanations.concept: Should a city burn its waste to make electricity?
explanations.description: A waste-to-energy plant burns mixed waste in a furnace and uses the heat to make electricity. Some Indian cities have built such plants, and people disagree about them.
examples: Delhi has several waste-to-energy plants. People living near the one at Okhla have gone to court about its smoke.
Sweden and Japan burn a large part of their waste in plants with strong filters.
Indian city waste is about half wet waste, which burns poorly.

perspectives.explanation: The dumps are full and growing. Burning shrinks waste to about a tenth of its volume and makes electricity. Modern plants have filters that catch most of the smoke and poisons.

perspectives.who: Residents and waste pickers who oppose them
perspectives.explanation: Indian waste is wet and burns badly. So plants add fuel, or burn paper and plastic that could be recycled. Filters are costly to run and are not always kept working. The ash is hazardous and still needs a landfill.
Burning has a small place, for the dry waste that truly cannot be recycled. It should come after segregation, composting and recycling, and never replace them.

explanations.art: A waste-to-energy plant with a tall chimney next to blocks of flats, and people on a balcony looking at it.

explanations.concept: There is no 'away': the same atoms go round
explanations.definition: Matter is not made or destroyed when waste rots, burns or is buried. Its atoms only move to a new place and join in new ways.
explanations.description: The Earth has had almost the same atoms for more than four billion years. Living beings pass them round. A leaf falls, decomposers eat it, and its atoms go into soil, air and new plants. In a forest there is no waste heap, because every leftover is food for someone. Human waste breaks this pattern in two ways. First, we gather huge amounts in one place, faster than decomposers can work. Second, we make materials such as plastic that decomposers have never met. So the question about any waste is where its atoms will go next, and how long that will take. The same is true beyond the Earth. Tens of thousands of pieces of old rockets and dead satellites now circle the Earth, and nobody planned where they would go.
examples: The carbon in a banana peel can be in the air next month, and in a spinach leaf next year.
A glass bottle thrown in a lake is still glass for a very, very long time.
A plastic bag does not rot. It cracks into smaller and smaller pieces of the same plastic.
explanations.art: A circle of arrows joining a leaf, a mushroom, soil, a seedling and a child eating, with a plastic bottle lying outside the circle.

agreed.text: Matter is never destroyed. When waste rots or burns, its atoms move into the air, the water or the soil.
agreed.evidence: Chemists since Lavoisier in the 1780s have weighed things before and after burning in sealed vessels. The total mass stays the same.

agreed.text: Organic waste that rots without air gives off methane, and methane traps heat in the air.
agreed.evidence: Gas collected from pipes sunk into landfills is about half methane. Satellites can now see methane rising from large dumps, including ones in India.

agreed.text: Plastic does not rot away in any time people have measured. It cracks into smaller pieces.
agreed.evidence: Plastic things many decades old are still pulled out of the sea with their printing readable. Microplastics are found from mountain snow to the deep sea.

agreed.text: Burning waste in the open sends smoke and poisonous gases into the air.
agreed.evidence: Smoke from open fires and burning dumps holds fine specks and gases such as dioxins, which people nearby breathe in.

agreed.text: Waste that is kept apart at home is much easier to compost and to recycle.
agreed.evidence: Cities such as Indore and Alappuzha compost or recycle most of their waste, and both began with segregation at home. Mixed waste gives dirty compost and paper nobody will buy.

agreed.text: Glass and metals can be recycled again and again without getting worse.
agreed.evidence: Melted glass and melted aluminium are the same materials as before. Much of the aluminium ever made is still in use today.

challenging.claim: Burning waste gets rid of it.
challenging.who: A common belief, and the reason many people burn leaves and litter
challenging.for: The heap really does shrink to a little ash, and the smell and flies go.
challenging.against: The matter has only moved. Most of it is now in the air as gases and smoke, which people breathe. Burning plastic also makes poisons. Dry leaves can be composted instead.
challenging.context: This card is about the belief that a fire makes waste disappear.

challenging.claim: If a packet has the triangle of arrows on it, it will be recycled.
challenging.for: The triangle looks like the recycling sign, and some marked things, such as drink bottles, are widely recycled.
challenging.against: The number in the triangle only names the kind of plastic. Whether a thing is recycled depends on someone collecting it, sorting it and finding a buyer. Up to 2015, only about 9 kilograms of every 100 kilograms of plastic had been recycled.
challenging.context: This card is about what the small triangle with a number on plastic things really tells you.

challenging.claim: A paper bag is always better for the Earth than a plastic bag.
challenging.who: A common belief. Studies by Britain's Environment Agency in 2011 and others tested it
challenging.for: Paper rots, and a loose paper bag does not choke a cow or a turtle. Plastic bags last for lifetimes.
challenging.against: Making a paper bag takes more water and energy than making a thin plastic bag. Trees are cut for it too. The British study found that a paper bag must be used at least 3 times to harm the climate less. A cotton bag must be used more than 100 times.
challenging.context: This card is about whether swapping plastic bags for paper bags is always the better choice.

challenging.claim: Food waste is natural, so it does no harm wherever it is thrown.
challenging.for: Food waste rots and becomes soil. In a compost pot or a field it feeds plants.
challenging.against: The place matters. In a pond, rotting food uses up the oxygen and fish die. Deep in a dump, it makes methane and leachate. At an open bin it brings rats and flies.
challenging.context: This card is about the belief that organic waste is harmless anywhere.

challenging.claim: Litter is the fault of the people who drop it, so they alone should fix it.
challenging.who: Many companies and city notices say this. People who study waste often disagree
challenging.for: Every wrapper on the road was dropped by someone. If each person used a bin, streets would be clean.
challenging.against: A person can only choose among the packets that are sold. A company that sells a snack in a packet nobody can recycle has already decided what waste there will be. India's rules now make such companies pay to collect their plastic back.
challenging.context: This card is about who is responsible for packaging waste: the person who buys or the company that makes.

challenging.claim: Plastic is the worst material, and we should stop using it.
challenging.for: Plastic lasts for lifetimes, harms animals and breaks into microplastics that are now found everywhere.
challenging.against: Plastic is light, cheap and safe for blood bags, syringes, helmets and water pipes. A glass bottle is much heavier, so lorries burn more fuel to carry it. The harm comes mostly from plastic that is used once for a few minutes.
challenging.context: This card is about whether the problem is plastic itself, or the way plastic is used.

big_questions.q: A newspaper is waste in your home and goods in the kabadiwala's shop. So is 'waste' a kind of thing, or a decision someone makes?
big_questions.hint: Think of one thing that was waste in your home last week. Who would have wanted it?

big_questions.q: If atoms are never destroyed, where are the atoms of a peel you threw out a year ago? Could some be in you?
big_questions.hint: Follow the peel in Where Did the Peel Go. Some atoms went into the air, and plants take in air.

big_questions.q: Plastic is made from oil, and oil formed from sea beings who died millions of years ago. Is plastic natural?
big_questions.hint: Ask what 'natural' means. Is it about where the atoms came from, or about who put them together?

big_questions.q: A forest has no dustbin and no dump. Why does a city need both?
big_questions.hint: Count who eats a fallen leaf in a forest. Then ask who eats a chips packet.

big_questions.q: Who should pay for a packet's ending: the company that made it, the person who bought it, or the city?
big_questions.hint: Think about who chose the material, who used it, and who has to live beside the dump.

big_questions.q: The people who make the least waste often live nearest the dump. Is that fair? What would make it fairer?
big_questions.hint: Think about who decides where a dump goes, and whose well it is near.

story.title: The Drum of Water
story.note: Yazhini, Vasanthi Athai, Selvi Akka, Kathir and their sorting shed are made up. The science is real. Drink-bottle plastic sinks in water and takeaway-box plastic floats. Recycling factories really do separate plastic flakes in tanks of water. Skilled sorters really can tell plastics apart by their sound and feel. 'Athai' is Tamil for a father's sister, 'akka' means older sister and 'thambi' means younger brother.
text: Every May, when school closed, Yazhini went to stay with her aunt in Coimbatore. Her aunt, Vasanthi Athai, ran a sorting shed for dry waste behind the vegetable market. Eleven women worked there. Lorries brought sacks from four thousand homes, and the women turned the sacks into neat bales that factories paid for.
Yazhini loved the shed. It smelled of dust and old paper, not of rot, because the homes on this route kept their wet waste apart.
Athai had one skill that Yazhini thought was magic. She could sort plastic with her eyes shut.

"Give me anything," Athai would say, and tie a towel over her eyes. Yazhini put a water bottle in her hands. Athai squeezed it once. It crackled, sharp and loud. "Bottle plastic. Number one." A shampoo bottle gave a dull knock. "Number two." A takeaway box bent with a soft click. "Five."
"How do you know?" Yazhini asked, every time.

"Thirty years," said Athai. "They look alike, kanna. They are not alike. Each one has its own voice. And the factory wants each one alone. Bottle plastic melted with box plastic comes out cloudy and weak. Nobody buys that."

That summer the shed had a new machine. The women had saved for two years to buy it. It was a green shredder, as tall as Yazhini, and it chopped plastic into flakes the size of a fingernail. A factory in Tiruppur paid nearly double for flakes, because flakes were easy to wash and melt.
On Thursday, a lorry was due at four o'clock to take the first load of clear bottle flake. Two hundred kilograms.
At noon Yazhini heard Athai's voice go very quiet, which was worse than shouting.

Kathir, the new helper, stood by the shredder with an empty sack in each hand. He was nineteen and had worked in the shed for six days. One sack had held clear bottles. The other had held clear takeaway boxes. He had tipped both into the machine together.
"They were both clear," he said. "I thought clear goes with clear."
On the floor lay one glittering heap of flakes. Athai picked up a handful and let it run through her fingers. Every flake was clear. Every flake was the size of a fingernail.
She squeezed one beside her ear. Then another. Yazhini watched her face. A flake was too small to crackle. It had no voice.
"Can we pick them apart?" Kathir asked.
Selvi Akka, the oldest sorter, laughed without smiling. "There are more flakes in that heap than there are people in Coimbatore. Start now, thambi. You will finish when you are a grandfather."

They tried anyway. All the women sat round the heap. Some flakes bent a little more than others, if you pressed them with a thumbnail. After half an hour, Yazhini had a pile the size of a lemon, and she was not sure of half of it. The heap looked the same as before.
"Mixed flake sells for a quarter of the price," Athai said. "If it sells." She did not look at Kathir. Kathir looked at the floor.
Yazhini's hands were grey with dust and stuck all over with flakes. She went out to the big blue drum by the tap, where everyone washed, and plunged her hands in up to the wrists.
The flakes came off her skin. She watched them, because there was nothing else to watch.
Some of them sank. They tipped and slid down through the water like tiny panes of glass, and settled on the bottom of the drum.
The others did not sink. They stayed at the top. She pushed one under with her finger. It came straight back up.

Yazhini stood very still. Then she ran inside and took a whole bottle and a whole box from the sacks by the door. She snipped a piece from each with Athai's big scissors and dropped both into the drum.
The bottle piece sank. The box piece floated.
She did it again with two more pieces, because one try can be a fluke. Sink. Float.
"Athai!" she shouted. "Athai, come and see. The water can tell them apart."
Vasanthi Athai came out, wiping her hands on her sari. She looked into the drum for a long moment. She pushed a floating flake down with one finger and watched it rise. Then she turned round.
"Selvi! Bring every drum and bucket we have. Kathir, the hose. And the big sieve from the kitchen, the one for draining rice."

They filled five drums. They poured the flakes in, a bucket at a time, and stirred with a stick so that no air bubble could hold a flake up. The box flakes rose in a pale layer. Kathir skimmed them off with the rice sieve. The bottle flakes lay on the bottom like wet sand, and the women scooped them out and spread them on sacks in the sun.
The May sun dried them in an hour. At ten minutes to four, Selvi Akka tied the last sack.
The lorry driver weighed the load and wrote in his book. "Clean flake," he said. "Cleaner than the big units send."
When he had gone, Kathir came and stood beside Yazhini at the drum. "Show me," he said. "From the beginning. Why does one sink?"

Yazhini cut two new pieces and put one in each of his hands. "Feel them. They are the same size. But the bottle piece is heavier than the same amount of water, so it sinks. The box piece is lighter than the same amount of water, so it floats. Your eyes can't see that. The water can."
Kathir dropped them in and watched.
Athai sat down on an upturned crate. "Thirty years I have listened to plastic," she said. "And all that time the answer was standing here in the washing drum."
The water in the drum grew still. One last flake, caught on the rim, slipped in. Yazhini watched to see which way it would go.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the turn comes when the flakes wash off Yazhini's hands and some sink while others float. Two plastics that look exactly alike are different materials with different densities. Bottle plastic is denser than water, and box plastic is less dense. Athai's ears could tell whole bottles apart, but only water could sort a heap of tiny flakes. Recycling works only when each material is alone, and density is one way to get it alone.
ask: Kathir thought clear plastic goes with clear plastic. What does a recycling factory need to know that colour does not tell?
Why could the women not sort the heap of flakes by hand in time?
Why did Yazhini drop a second pair of pieces in the drum before she called her aunt?
The women stirred the drums with a stick. What could go wrong if they had not?
What other mixed-up things could you separate with a bucket of water? What could you not?

games.title: A Hundred Years Later
games.context: This is a card game about what happens to waste over a long time. Each card names a thing and the place where it was thrown. You say where that thing will be in a hundred years.

printables.title: 16 two-sided cards to cut out (the answer is on the back)

items.f: A banana peel in a balcony compost pot, mixed with dry leaves.
items.b: ROTTED AWAY. Decomposers with plenty of air ate the peel in a few weeks. The atoms are now in soil, air and plants.

items.f: A glass pickle bottle sold to the kabadiwala.
items.b: MADE INTO SOMETHING NEW. Glass can be crushed, melted and remade again and again. It may have been many bottles by now.

items.f: A glass bottle thrown into a lake.
items.b: STILL THERE. Nobody eats glass, and water does not dissolve it. It may be broken, but it is still glass.

items.f: A thin plastic carry bag blown into a field.
items.b: IN SMALL PIECES. Sunlight made the bag brittle and it cracked into microplastics. Every piece is still plastic.
MADE INTO SOMETHING NEW. The paper became a box or an egg tray. After five to seven rounds its fibres were too short, and they rotted.

items.f: An aluminium drink can sold as scrap.
items.b: MADE INTO SOMETHING NEW. Aluminium can be melted and remade without end. Remelting takes about one twentieth of the energy of making new metal.

items.f: A cotton shirt buried in damp soil.
items.b: ROTTED AWAY. Cotton is made by a plant, so fungi and bacteria can eat it. It was gone within a few years.

items.f: A polyester shirt buried in the same damp soil.
items.b: STILL THERE. Polyester is a plastic, the same kind as a drink bottle. Decomposers cannot eat it.

items.f: A shiny chips packet dropped in a street drain.
items.b: STILL THERE or IN SMALL PIECES. Either answer scores. The packet is plastic with a metal coat, so it does not rot. It may have helped to block the drain.

items.f: A clear drink bottle, marked 1, sold to the kabadiwala.
items.b: MADE INTO SOMETHING NEW. It was most likely made into polyester fibre for cloth. That cloth was not made into bottles again, so this is downcycling.

items.f: A used pencil-cell battery thrown on an open dump.
items.b: IN SMALL PIECES. The steel case rusted open, and the metals inside leaked into the soil and the water under the dump.

items.f: A coconut shell left under a tree.
items.b: ROTTED AWAY. A coconut shell is hard and rots slowly, over some years. But a plant made it, so decomposers can eat it.

items.f: A thermocol plate thrown into the sea.
items.b: IN SMALL PIECES. Waves broke the plate into tiny beads. Fish and birds may have swallowed some. Each bead is still plastic.

items.f: A bucket of leftover rice tipped into a small pond.
items.b: ROTTED AWAY. Microbes ate the rice in days. They used up the oxygen in the water as they fed, so fish may have died.

items.f: A clay tea cup dropped by the railway track.
items.b: IN SMALL PIECES. Baked clay does not rot, but it crumbles back into bits like the soil it came from. It poisons nobody.

items.f: A steel tumbler that a family uses every day.
items.b: STILL THERE, and still in use. A thing that lasts and stays wanted never becomes waste at all.

printables.title: The four answers (each player copies these onto four slips of paper)

rules: Shuffle the 16 cards and put them in a pile, question side up.
One player reads the top card aloud. The card names a thing and where it was thrown.
Everyone thinks for ten seconds. On the count of three, each player holds up one answer slip.
Turn the card over and read the back. Each player with the right answer scores 1 point.
A player who can also say why scores 1 more point. The reader decides whether the reason is good.
Take turns to be the reader. Stop when all 16 cards have been read. The most points wins.
Playing alone: sort the 16 cards into four piles, one for each answer. Then turn them over and count how many are right.

setup.art: Sixteen cut-out cards in a pile on a table, with four small paper slips beside it marked with the four answers.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards. Write the four answers on four slips for each player.

setup.art: Two children and a parent each holding up one paper slip at the same moment, while one child reads a card.
setup.caption: 2. Read a card. On the count of three, hold up your answer.

setup.art: The card turned over to show the answer, with a pencil and a score sheet beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over. Score 1 for the answer and 1 for the reason.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 16 cards. 2. Give each player four slips of paper. 3. Each player writes one answer on each slip: ROTTED AWAY, STILL THERE, IN SMALL PIECES, MADE INTO SOMETHING NEW. 4. Shuffle the cards and put them question side up.
flow.say: Each card names a thing and a place. We have to say where that thing will be in a hundred years. There are only four answers.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Write the four answers on four slips. Shuffle the cards. Put them question side up.
flow.context: This is the first step of A Hundred Years Later. Here you cut out the cards and write the four answers on slips.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to read the top card aloud. 2. Count to three, and everyone holds up one slip. 3. Turn the card over and read the back. 4. Give 1 point for the right answer and 1 more for a good reason.
flow.say: Listen to the thing and the place. Both matter. Which answer will you hold up? Why did you choose it?
flow.kid: Read the top card aloud. Think about the thing and the place. Hold up one slip. Turn the card over. Score your points.

ask.q: Two cards have a glass bottle, and two have a shirt. Why are their answers different?
good: The glass bottle went to two different places: a kabadiwala and a lake.
The two shirts are different materials. Cotton rots and polyester does not.
So the answer depends on the material and on the place.

flow.parent: A good reason names the material and the place. For example: 'Cotton comes from a plant, so decomposers can eat it.' The chips packet card accepts two answers.
flow.context: This is the main part of A Hundred Years Later. Here you read each card, hold up an answer and check the back.

flow.do: 1. Count the points. 2. Lay out the cards that were got wrong. 3. Ask which things were never waste at all, and which will outlast everyone in the room.
flow.say: Which card surprised you? Which of these things will still be here after all of us are gone?
flow.kid: Count your points. Which card surprised you? Which things will outlast all of us?

check.q: A cotton shirt and a polyester shirt are buried in the same damp soil. After many years, what is left?
options: Only the polyester shirt is left
Only the cotton shirt is left
check.why: Cotton is made by a plant, so decomposers can eat it. Polyester is a plastic, and decomposers cannot. Choosing 'both have rotted' means thinking that all cloth is one material.

flow.context: This is the last step of A Hundred Years Later. Here you count the points and talk about the cards that surprised you.

games.title: The Last Landfill
games.context: In this game you run a city for eight years. The city has one landfill with 25 spaces. Each year you get 3 coins to spend on ways to keep waste out of the landfill.

printables.title: 24 waste cards to cut out
items: WET: tea leaves and coffee grounds
WET: dry leaves swept from a yard
WET: spoilt food from a wedding hall
PAPER: paper bags from a shop

printables.title: City sheet: copy this onto paper
items: LANDFILL: draw 25 empty boxes in a row. Tick one box for each card that goes to the landfill.
COINS: write how many coins you have. You get 3 new coins at the start of each year.
SORTING AT HOME, costs 3 coins. Nothing else works until you have bought this.
COMPOST PLANT, costs 4 coins. Every WET card goes here.
DRY WASTE CENTRE, costs 4 coins. Every PAPER, BOTTLE and GLASS AND METAL card goes here.
HAZARD COLLECTION, costs 2 coins. Every HAZARD card goes here.
PACKET RULE, costs 5 coins. Companies must take back their packets. Every PACKET card goes back to them.
YEARS: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8. Cross one off after each year.

rules: Copy the city sheet onto paper. Shuffle the 24 waste cards and put them face down.
At the start of each year, add 3 coins to your coins. You may buy things from the city sheet, or save.
You must buy SORTING AT HOME before anything else. Mixed waste cannot be composted or recycled.
Then turn over 6 waste cards. This is the city's waste for the year.
A card goes to a plant, centre, collection or rule you have bought. It does no harm there.
Every other card goes to the landfill. Tick 1 box for it. A HAZARD card in the landfill leaks, so tick 2 boxes.
When the pile runs out, shuffle all 24 cards and use them again.
If all 25 boxes are ticked before year 8 ends, the landfill is full and the city loses.
If boxes are still empty after year 8, the city wins. Your score is the number of empty boxes.
With friends: play as one city council. Talk over each choice and agree before you buy.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a row of 25 small boxes, a list of five things to buy with prices, and a pile of face-down cards beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Copy the city sheet. Shuffle the 24 waste cards.

setup.art: A child placing three coins on the sheet and pointing to 'SORTING AT HOME, 3 coins'.
setup.caption: 2. Each year, take 3 coins and decide what to buy.

setup.art: Six waste cards turned face up, four pushed towards the words 'COMPOST PLANT' and two towards the row of boxes, where a pencil ticks two boxes.
setup.caption: 3. Turn over 6 cards. Tick a landfill box for each card that has nowhere else to go.

flow.do: 1. Copy the city sheet onto paper, with 25 boxes for the landfill. 2. Cut out the 24 waste cards and shuffle them. 3. Read the rules aloud together. 4. Ask what the city should buy first, and why.
flow.say: You are the city council. The landfill has only 25 spaces, and the city makes 6 cards of waste a year. What will you buy first? Why?
flow.kid: Copy the city sheet. Draw 25 boxes for the landfill. Shuffle the waste cards. Decide what to buy first.
flow.parent: With nothing bought, the landfill takes at least 6 boxes a year and is full in the fifth year. Sorting at home must come first. After that, the dry waste centre takes 10 of the 24 cards and the compost plant takes 8. These two matter most.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Last Landfill. Here you set up the city sheet and the waste cards, and plan what to buy first.

flow.do: 1. Each year, take 3 coins and buy or save. 2. Turn over 6 cards. 3. Send each card to something you have bought, or to the landfill. 4. Tick the landfill boxes. 5. Cross off the year. 6. Play 8 years, or until the landfill is full.
flow.say: It is a new year, so add three new coins. Will you buy something now, or save for something bigger? Then turn over six cards. Where can each card go?
flow.kid: Take 3 coins. Buy or save. Turn over 6 cards. Send each card somewhere. Tick the landfill boxes. Play 8 years.

ask.q: Which kind of card filled most of the landfill boxes in the first years?
good: Wet waste, because there are 8 wet cards out of 24.
Everything, because before sorting at home, every card went to the landfill.

ask.q: Which cards still went to the landfill after you built the compost plant and the dry waste centre?
good: The packets, because no centre can recycle them.
The hazard cards, until we bought the hazard collection.

flow.parent: A good order is this. Buy sorting at home in year 1 and save in year 2. Buy the compost plant and the dry waste centre in years 3 and 4. The hazard collection and the packet rule come after. That usually ends with about 20 boxes ticked. Buying the packet rule or the hazard collection before the two big plants often fills the landfill by year 8.
flow.context: This is the main part of The Last Landfill. Each year you spend coins and turn over 6 waste cards. You tick a landfill box for each card with nowhere else to go.

flow.do: 1. Count the empty boxes. 2. Ask which purchase saved the most boxes. 3. Ask what the game leaves out. 4. Play again with a different order, and compare the scores.
flow.say: How many boxes are still empty? Which thing you bought saved the most space? What does a real city have to think about that this game leaves out?
flow.kid: Count the empty boxes. Which thing you bought saved the most space? What does the game leave out?

ask.q: What does a real city have to think about that this game leaves out?
good: People have to agree to sort their waste. Coins cannot buy that.
The compost and the recycled things need buyers.
The people who collect and sort the waste need fair pay and safe work.
A real city makes more waste every year.

check.q: In The Last Landfill, why must SORTING AT HOME be bought before the compost plant?
options: It is the cheapest thing to buy
Mixed waste cannot be composted or recycled
The rules were made up that way
check.why: A compost plant needs wet waste with no plastic or glass in it. A recycler needs dry waste with no food on it. Both need the waste kept apart at home. Choosing 'makes the waste smaller' mixes up sorting with crushing.

flow.context: This is the last step of The Last Landfill. Here you count the empty boxes and talk about which choice helped most.

experiments.title: The Float Tank Test: can water sort plastics that look alike?
experiments.context: In this experiment you cut small pieces from the plastic things in your dry waste. You drop them in water to see which sink and which float. Then you use water to sort a mixed heap of look-alike flakes.
experiments.question: Do all kinds of plastic do the same thing in water? Can water separate two plastics that look the same?
experiments.predict: Guess first. You will push small pieces of a bottle, a cap, a milk packet and a takeaway box under water. Will they all float, all sink, or will some do each? Why do you think so? Write your guess and your reason.
experiments.fair_test: Every piece is about the same size, 2 centimetres across. Every piece is pushed under the same water for 5 seconds, so that no air bubble holds a piece up. Two pieces of each thing are tested, because one piece can be a fluke.

materials.item: an empty clear plastic drink bottle, with its cap and the loose ring under the cap
a rinsed and dried milk packet or oil packet
a clear or white plastic takeaway box, or a curd cup
other clean plastic things from the dry waste, such as a shampoo bottle, a disposable spoon or a bottle label
strong scissors
a large clear bowl, or a steel vessel, holding about 1 litre of water
a clear glass tumbler
dish-washing liquid
salt
a spoon and a tea strainer
an old newspaper, a pencil and a notebook

experiments.safety: Cut plastic has sharp corners. A grown-up cuts the bottle and the hard pieces. Use only clean, rinsed plastic, and wash your hands with soap at the end.

schedule.what: Read the numbers, cut the pieces and guess. Test each plastic in plain water, then the sinkers in salt water. Sort a mixed heap of flakes with water and explain the result.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for every thing you tested. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
example_chart.note: These results are made up, to show what a finished table can look like. Your things and your results may be different.

setup.art: Six small heaps of cut plastic squares on a newspaper, each heap beside the thing it was cut from and a pencilled number.
setup.caption: 1. Read the number on each thing. Cut two small pieces from each.

setup.art: A child pushing a clear plastic square under the water in a glass bowl with the back of a spoon.
setup.caption: 2. Push each piece under water for 5 seconds. Let go and watch.

setup.art: The same bowl seen from the side: clear pieces lying on the bottom and blue and white pieces floating on top.
setup.caption: 3. Write down which pieces sink and which float.

setup.art: A tea strainer lifting floating flakes off the top of a bowl, with other flakes lying on the bottom.
setup.caption: 4. Mix two kinds of flakes. Let the water sort them, and skim off the floaters.

flow.do: 1. Lay the plastic things on the newspaper. 2. Find the small triangle on each one. It is often on the base. 3. Read the number inside and write it in the table. 4. If a thing has no number, write 'none'.
flow.say: Every one of these is called plastic. Let's see if they are marked the same. Find the little triangle and read the number inside.
flow.kid: Find the small triangle on each plastic thing. Read the number inside. Write it in your table. Write 'none' if there is no number.
flow.parent: A drink bottle is marked 1. Caps are usually 2 or 5, and often have no mark. Milk packets are 4. Takeaway boxes and most curd cups are 5. Shampoo bottles are 2. Some disposable cups and spoons are 6.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Float Tank Test. Here you find the number in the triangle on each plastic thing.

flow.do: 1. Cut two squares, about 2 centimetres across, from the wall of the drink bottle. 2. Snip the loose ring from under the cap into two pieces. 3. Cut two squares from each other thing. 4. Put each pair on the newspaper beside the thing it came from.
flow.say: I will cut the hard ones. We need two small pieces of each thing, all about the same size. Keep each pair beside the thing it came from.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to cut the pieces. You need two small squares from each thing. Keep each pair beside its own thing.
flow.parent: Pierce the bottle wall with the scissor tip first, then cut. The ring under the cap is the same plastic as the cap and is much easier to cut. Do not use thermocol, which is full of air.
flow.context: This step of the Float Tank Test is for cutting. A grown-up cuts two small pieces, about 2 centimetres across, from each plastic thing.

flow.do: 1. Fill the bowl with about 1 litre of water. 2. Add 2 drops of dish-washing liquid and stir gently, without making foam. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason for each thing. 4. Write the guesses in the table.
flow.say: All of these are plastic. When we push the pieces under water, will they all float, all sink, or will some do each? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at your pieces. Will they all float? Will they all sink? Or some of each? Say why. Write a guess for each thing.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: They will all float, because plastic is light. (A fair guess. The test will show.)
The thick ones will sink and the thin ones will float.
They might differ, because they have different numbers.

flow.parent: The soap stops small flat pieces from resting on the skin of the water. Do not correct the guesses.
flow.context: This step of the Float Tank Test is for guessing. You guess which plastic pieces will float and which will sink, and say why.

flow.do: 1. Take the two pieces of one thing. 2. Push both under the water with the back of the spoon and count to 5. 3. Take the spoon away and count slowly to 20. 4. Write 'floats' or 'sinks' in the table. 5. Lift the pieces out with the tea strainer. 6. Do the same for each thing.
flow.say: Push both pieces right under and hold them for five seconds. Now let go. Watch where each one settles.
flow.kid: Push two pieces under water with the spoon. Count to 5. Let go. Count to 20. Write 'floats' or 'sinks'. Test every thing.

ask.q: Did the two pieces of the same thing always do the same?
good: Yes, both bottle pieces sank and both cap pieces floated.
One floated at first, but it had a bubble on it. When I pushed it again, it sank.

flow.parent: The drink bottle pieces sink. The cap ring, the milk packet, the takeaway box and the shampoo bottle float. A piece marked 6 sinks slowly. If the two pieces of one thing disagree, look for an air bubble. Rub it off and push the piece under again.
flow.context: This is the main step of the Float Tank Test. Here you push the pieces of each plastic under water and record which sink and which float.

flow.do: 1. Fill the glass tumbler with 200 millilitres of water. 2. Add 6 level teaspoons of salt and stir for 2 minutes, until almost all of it dissolves. 3. Drop in one piece of each plastic that sank in plain water. 4. Push it under, let go and watch. 5. Write the result in the last column.
flow.say: Salt water is denser than plain water. Will a piece that sank in plain water also sink in salt water? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Stir 6 teaspoons of salt into a tumbler of water. Drop in each piece that sank before. Does it still sink? Write what you see.
flow.parent: The drink bottle piece still sinks. A solid piece marked 6 rises to the top, because it is only a little denser than plain water. You may have nothing marked 6 at home. Then the finding is simply that bottle plastic sinks even in salt water.
flow.context: This step of the Float Tank Test uses salt water. You test whether the pieces that sank in plain water also sink in strong salt water.

flow.do: 1. Cut 10 small flakes, about 1 centimetre across, from the clear drink bottle. 2. Cut 10 flakes of the same size from the takeaway box or the milk packet. 3. Mix all 20 in your hand. 4. Give your child 30 seconds to sort them by eye into two heaps. 5. Then tip all 20 into the bowl, stir and wait until the water is still. 6. Skim off the floaters with the tea strainer. Count each group.
flow.say: Here are twenty flakes, mixed up. You have thirty seconds to sort them by looking. Now let's give the same job to the water.
flow.kid: Mix 10 bottle flakes with 10 box flakes. Try to sort them by eye in 30 seconds. Then tip them in the water. Stir. Skim off the floaters. Count them.
flow.parent: There should be 10 flakes on the bottom and 10 on top. If a clear takeaway box is used, the two kinds look almost the same in the hand. Recycling factories sort flakes this way, in long tanks of water.
flow.context: This step of the Float Tank Test mixes two plastics. You try to sort 20 small flakes by eye, and then let water sort them.

flow.do: 1. Look at the whole table together. 2. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. 3. Only then, explain density. 4. Ask what the numbers 1, 2, 4 and 5 turned out to mean.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why did it happen?
flow.kid: Look at your table. Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: All the pieces were about the same size. So why did some sink and some float?
good: They are different materials. Some are denser than water and some are less dense.
The bottle plastic packs more matter into the same space.

ask.q: A factory gets a sack of mixed bottles and caps, all chopped small. How could it separate them?
good: Tip them into a tank of water. The bottle bits sink and the cap bits float.

flow.parent: Density is how much matter is packed into each bit of space. Bottle plastic is about one and a third times as dense as water. Cap, packet and box plastics are a little less dense than water.

check.q: In the Float Tank Test, a bottle piece sank and a cap piece of the same size floated. What does this show?
options: The two pieces are different materials
The bottle piece had water inside it
check.why: Two pieces of the same size did different things in the same water, so the materials must differ. Bottle plastic is denser than water and cap plastic is less dense. Choosing 'thinner' or 'coloured' means looking at shape or colour, which make no difference to floating.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Float Tank Test. Here you explain why some plastics sank and others floated.

experiments.title: Scrunch and Peel: is a shiny packet metal, plastic or both?
experiments.context: In this experiment you test shiny wrappers to find out what they are made of. You scrunch them, shine a torch through them, and peel a juice carton into its layers.
experiments.question: A chips packet is silver inside, like kitchen foil. Is it made of metal? And is a juice carton made only of paper?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which of your shiny wrappers are metal, like kitchen foil, and which are plastic? How many different materials are in the wall of a juice carton? Why do you think so? Write your guesses and your reasons.
experiments.fair_test: Every wrapper gets the same two tests. Each piece is about 10 centimetres across. Each is squeezed in a fist for 5 seconds, then left for 10 seconds. Each is pressed flat on the same torch in the same dim room.
results_table: Scrunch test: stays or springs open
Torch test: light comes through or not

materials.item: a piece of kitchen aluminium foil, or the foil lid of a curd cup, about 10 centimetres across
an empty chips or mixture packet, wiped clean and dry
an empty biscuit wrapper that is shiny inside
a toffee or chocolate wrapper
an empty juice, milk or buttermilk carton, the kind kept on a shelf, rinsed
a torch, or the torch of a phone
scissors
a bowl of warm water from the tap
a notebook and a pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts the carton, because its wall is stiff. Use only empty, wiped packets, and wash your hands with soap at the end.

schedule.what: Guess what each wrapper is made of. Do the scrunch test and the torch test. Soak and peel a piece of carton, count its layers and explain the results.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for every wrapper. Stick one small piece of each carton layer in your notebook and label it. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
example_chart.note: These results are made up, to show what a finished table can look like. Your wrappers may give different results.

setup.art: A sheet of kitchen foil, an opened chips packet, a biscuit wrapper and a toffee wrapper laid flat in a row, shiny side up.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the wrappers and guess which are metal.

setup.art: Two fists opening: in one a tight ball of foil, in the other a chips packet springing back open.
setup.caption: 2. Scrunch each wrapper for 5 seconds. Does it stay in a ball?

setup.art: A piece of chips packet pressed over a phone torch in a dim room, with a faint glow showing through it.
setup.caption: 3. Press each wrapper on a torch. Does any light come through?

setup.art: A square of juice carton peeled at one corner into a clear film, a thick paper layer and a silver layer.
setup.caption: 4. Soak a piece of carton and peel it into its layers.

flow.do: 1. Open each packet flat and wipe it dry. 2. Cut a piece about 10 centimetres across from each. 3. Lay the pieces in a row, shiny side up. 4. Ask which are metal and which are plastic, and why. 5. Write the guesses in the table.
flow.say: These are all silver and shiny. Which do you think are metal, like the kitchen foil? Which are plastic? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Lay the wrappers in a row, shiny side up. Which are metal? Which are plastic? Say why. Write your guesses.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: They are all metal, because they are all shiny silver. (A fair guess. The test will show.)
The chips packet is plastic, because it stretches before it tears.

flow.context: This is the first step of Scrunch and Peel. Here you lay out the shiny wrappers and guess what each is made of.

flow.do: 1. Squeeze the kitchen foil into a tight ball in one fist and count to 5. 2. Put the ball on the table and count to 10. 3. Write whether it stays a ball or springs open. 4. Do the same with each wrapper.
flow.say: Squeeze it as tight as you can for five seconds. Now put it down and watch it for ten seconds. What does it do?
flow.kid: Squeeze each wrapper into a tight ball. Count to 5. Put it down. Count to 10. Does it stay a ball? Write what you see.
flow.parent: Metal foil stays in a tight ball. A plastic film springs open, even when it has a metal coat. Chips packets and most biscuit wrappers spring open.
flow.context: This step of Scrunch and Peel is the scrunch test. You squeeze each wrapper into a ball and see whether the ball stays or springs open.

flow.do: 1. Make the room dim. 2. Switch on the torch and press the kitchen foil flat over it. 3. Look for any light coming through. 4. Do the same with each wrapper. 5. Write the results.
flow.say: Press the foil flat over the torch. Can you see any light through it? Now try the chips packet.
flow.kid: Make the room dim. Press each wrapper flat on the torch. Does light come through? Write what you see.
flow.parent: No light passes through kitchen foil, unless it has a pinhole. A faint glow comes through a chips packet. Its metal coat is hundreds of times thinner than kitchen foil, so a little light gets through.
flow.context: This step of Scrunch and Peel is the torch test. You press each wrapper over a torch to see whether light comes through.

flow.do: 1. Cut a square about 6 centimetres across from the wall of the carton. 2. Soak it in warm water for 5 minutes. 3. Peel the square apart from one corner, as slowly as you can. 4. Rub the wet paper off the silver layer with a thumb. 5. Lay the layers side by side. 6. Do the scrunch test and the torch test on the silver layer.
flow.say: This carton feels like thick paper. Let's soak a piece and peel it apart. How many layers can you find?
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to cut a square of carton. Soak it for 5 minutes. Peel it apart slowly. Rub off the wet paper. Count the layers.

ask.q: How many different materials did you find, and what are they?
good: Three: a clear plastic film, thick paper and a silver metal layer.
The silver layer has plastic stuck to it too.

flow.parent: You should find a thin clear film on the outside, a thick layer of paper, and a silver layer inside. The silver layer is real metal foil with plastic film stuck to it. It lets no light through, but it may spring open a little because of the plastic. About three quarters of a carton's mass is paper.
flow.context: This step of Scrunch and Peel takes a juice carton apart. You soak a square of carton and peel it into its layers.

flow.do: 1. Fill in the last column of the table for every wrapper. 2. Count how many materials each one has. 3. Ask which wrappers a factory could melt down as one material.
flow.say: Now we know what each one is made of. Which of these is one material only? Which are two or three stuck together?
flow.kid: Fill in what each wrapper is made of. Count the materials in each. Which wrapper is one material only?
flow.parent: Only the kitchen foil is one material. The chips packet and the carton are multi-layer packaging.
flow.context: This step of Scrunch and Peel sums up. You write what each wrapper is made of and count its materials.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. 2. Ask why a company would stick three materials together. 3. Ask what that does to recycling.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why did it happen?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: Why would a company stick paper, plastic and metal together?
good: Each layer does a job. Paper makes it stiff, plastic keeps liquid in, and metal keeps light and air out.
It keeps food fresh for months with very little material.

ask.q: Why is such a packet hard to recycle?
good: A factory needs one material at a time, and these layers cannot be pulled apart cheaply.

check.q: A chips packet is silver inside but springs open after you scrunch it. What is it made of?
options: Plastic film with a very thin metal coat
check.why: Metal foil stays scrunched, and plastic film springs back. The silver colour is a coat of aluminium far thinner than kitchen foil. Choosing 'thick metal foil' means judging by colour alone.

flow.context: This is the last step of Scrunch and Peel. Here you explain your results and think about why packets are made in layers.

experiments.title: The Crush Test: how much of our dry waste is air?
experiments.context: In this experiment you fill a bucket with clean dry waste and measure how high it comes. Then you flatten every piece, put it back and measure again.
experiments.question: A waste truck carries dry waste by the truckload. How much of that load is really waste, and how much is air inside bottles and boxes?
experiments.predict: Guess first. When every bottle, box and carton in the bucket is flattened, how high will the same waste come: about the same, about half, or less than half? Why do you think so? Write your guess and your reason.
experiments.fair_test: The same pieces of waste go into the same bucket both times. Nothing is added or taken away. Both times the waste is dropped in loosely and not pressed down from above.
results_table: Height of waste in the bucket (cm)

materials.item: clean, dry waste saved over 4 or 5 days: plastic bottles, cartons, cardboard boxes, cups and packets
a bucket of 10 to 15 litres
a ruler or a measuring tape
a notebook and a pencil

experiments.safety: Do not use tins or glass, because they have sharp edges when crushed. Use only rinsed, dry waste, and wash your hands with soap at the end.

schedule.what: Fill the bucket loosely and measure. Guess. Flatten every piece, refill and measure again. Work out how many times lower the waste is.

experiments.record: Write both heights in the table. Divide the first height by the second. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: height of the same waste in a bucket
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A bucket filled to the top with loose plastic bottles, a juice carton, two small boxes and paper cups, with a ruler standing inside it.
setup.caption: 1. Drop the dry waste loosely into a bucket. Measure how high it comes.

setup.art: A child in shoes pressing a capless plastic bottle flat on the floor, with flattened boxes stacked beside her.
setup.caption: 2. Take everything out and flatten each piece.

setup.art: The same bucket with a low stack of flattened waste at the bottom and the ruler showing a much smaller height.
setup.caption: 3. Put the flat pieces back. Measure the height again.

flow.do: 1. Count the pieces of dry waste. 2. Drop them one by one into the bucket, without pressing. 3. Stand the ruler inside the bucket, on the bottom. 4. Read the height at the top of the waste and write it down.
flow.say: Drop each piece in gently. Don't press. Now, how high does our waste come in the bucket?
flow.kid: Count the pieces. Drop them in the bucket gently. Do not press. Measure how high the waste comes. Write the height.
flow.parent: If the waste rises above the rim, take a few pieces out and count again. If it is uneven, measure to where most of the top lies.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Crush Test. Here you fill a bucket loosely with clean dry waste and measure its height.

flow.do: 1. Explain that every piece will be flattened and put back. 2. Ask how high the same waste will come then. 3. Ask for the reason. 4. Write the guess as a number of centimetres.
flow.say: We will flatten every piece and put it all back. How high will it come then? About the same, about half, or less? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Every piece will be flattened and put back. How high will the waste come then? Say why. Write your guess in centimetres.
flow.context: This step of the Crush Test is for guessing. You guess how high the same waste will come after it is flattened, and say why.

flow.do: 1. Tip the waste out. 2. Take the cap off each bottle, press the bottle flat under a shoe, and screw the cap back on. 3. Open the flaps of each carton and box and fold it flat. 4. Stack the cups inside each other. 5. Fold each packet flat. 6. Lay all the pieces back in the bucket, without pressing down.
flow.say: Take the cap off first, so the air can get out. Press the bottle flat, then put the cap back so it stays flat.
flow.kid: Take the cap off each bottle. Press it flat under your shoe. Put the cap back on. Fold boxes flat. Stack the cups. Lay everything back in the bucket.
flow.parent: A capped bottle will not flatten, because the air cannot get out. That is worth letting your child find out.
