flow.context: This is the main step of the Crush Test. Here you flatten every bottle, box and carton and put them all back in the bucket.

flow.do: 1. Stand the ruler in the bucket again and read the new height. 2. Write it in the table. 3. Divide the first height by the second height. 4. Say the answer as 'so many times lower'.
flow.say: Read the new height. Now divide the first height by this one. How many times lower is the flattened waste?
flow.kid: Measure the new height. Write it down. Divide the first height by the new height. How many times lower is it?
flow.parent: Most families find the flattened waste is 3 to 5 times lower. With many bottles the difference is larger. With mostly paper it is smaller.
flow.context: This step of the Crush Test measures the result. You measure the flattened waste and work out how many times lower it is.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. 2. Ask what was in the bucket the first time, besides waste. 3. Ask what this means for a waste truck.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why did it happen?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened. What does this mean for a waste truck?

ask.q: The amount of plastic and card did not change. So what left the bucket?
good: Air. The bottles and boxes were mostly full of air.
The space inside and between the pieces.

ask.q: What does this mean for the truck that collects dry waste?
good: A truck full of loose bottles is carrying mostly air.
If people flattened their waste, one truck could do the work of three or four.

check.q: In the Crush Test, flattened waste filled far less of the bucket. What changed?
options: The space the waste takes up
check.why: Flattening pushes the air out, so the waste takes up less space. Its mass, its material and the number of pieces all stay the same. Choosing 'mass' mixes up how heavy a thing is with how much room it takes.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Crush Test. Here you explain why the same waste took up so much less space.

activities.title: Once Alive or Never Alive: sort twelve things
activities.context: This short activity starts the unit. You sort twelve things from the kitchen and the dry waste by where their material came from. Then you guess which of them decomposers can eat.

materials.item: a fresh banana peel or vegetable peel, on a saucer
a sheet of newspaper, a cotton rag and a dry leaf or flower
a wooden ice-cream stick or a piece of coconut shell, and a clean eggshell
a glass jar, a steel spoon and a piece of aluminium foil
an empty plastic bottle and a rinsed milk packet
slips of paper and a pencil

activities.record: Draw the three groups in your notebook. Circle the things you think decomposers can eat.

setup.art: Twelve things spread on a table: a banana peel on a saucer, newspaper, a cotton rag, a dry leaf, an ice-cream stick, an eggshell, a glass jar, a steel spoon, foil, a plastic bottle and a milk packet.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out twelve things from the kitchen and the dry waste.

setup.art: The same things in three groups behind three paper labels: 'MADE BY A LIVING BEING', 'MADE FROM ROCK, SAND OR ORE' and 'NOT SURE'.
setup.caption: 2. Sort them by where their material came from.

flow.do: 1. Lay the twelve things on a table. 2. Write three labels: MADE BY A LIVING BEING, MADE FROM ROCK, SAND OR ORE, and NOT SURE. 3. Ask what your child notices about the things, before any sorting.
flow.say: Here are twelve things we might throw out. Look at them and touch them. What do you notice? What do you wonder?
flow.kid: Lay out the twelve things. Look at them and touch them. What do you notice? What do you wonder?
flow.context: This is the first step of Once Alive or Never Alive. Here you lay out twelve things and say what you notice about them.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to put each thing behind one label. 2. Ask for a reason each time. 3. Do not correct the choices yet. 4. Then ask which things decomposers could eat, and why.
flow.say: Where did the material of each thing come from? Did a plant or an animal make it? Or was it made from rock, sand or ore?
flow.kid: Put each thing behind one label. Say where its material came from. Then say which things decomposers can eat.

ask.q: Paper and cotton are dry. Why do they belong with the peel?
good: Paper is made from trees and cotton from a plant.
Decomposers can eat both, so they rot.

ask.q: Where did you put the plastic bottle, and why?
good: Not sure, because a factory made it.
With rock and ore, because it does not rot.

flow.parent: These were made by a living being: a peel, newspaper, cotton, a leaf, wood, a coconut shell and an eggshell. These were made from rock, sand or ore: glass, steel and foil. The eggshell is a good puzzle. A hen made it, but it is mostly a mineral, so it breaks down very slowly.
flow.context: This is the main step of Once Alive or Never Alive. Here you sort twelve things by where their material came from.

flow.do: 1. Tell your child that plastic is made from oil. 2. Say that oil formed from tiny sea beings who died millions of years ago. 3. Ask whether that changes where the bottle belongs. 4. Explain the words organic and inorganic.
flow.say: Plastic is made from oil. Oil formed from tiny sea beings who died millions of years ago. Does that change where you would put the bottle?
flow.kid: Plastic is made from oil. Oil formed from sea beings who died long ago. Where does the bottle belong now? Say why.
flow.parent: There is no single right place for the bottle. Its atoms came from living beings, but no decomposer can eat it. Waste rules treat plastic as inorganic waste, because it does not rot.

check.q: Why does a cotton rag rot, while a glass jar does not?
options: Cotton is soft and glass is hard
A plant made cotton, so decomposers can eat it
check.why: Decomposers have enzymes for what living beings make. Cotton is made by a plant, and glass is melted sand. Choosing 'soft and hard' does not work, because a hard coconut shell rots and a soft plastic bag does not.

flow.context: This is the last step of Once Alive or Never Alive. Here you learn where plastic comes from and the words organic and inorganic.

activities.title: The Scrap Price Chart: what is each material worth?
activities.context: In this activity you find out what a scrap dealer pays for one kilogram of each material. You draw a bar chart of the prices and work out why they differ so much.

materials.item: a notebook, a pencil and a ruler
a scrap dealer or kabadiwala to ask, or the example prices given in the second step

activities.record: Keep the price table and the bar chart. Under the chart, write which material is worth most and which is worth nothing, and why.

example_chart.title: Example scrap prices (they change by city and by month)
example_chart.note: These are example prices only. Ask a scrap dealer near you for today's prices.

setup.art: A child with a notebook asking a scrap dealer at a small shop stacked with newspapers, tins and bottles, with a hanging balance beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Ask a scrap dealer what one kilogram of each material sells for.

setup.art: A hand-drawn bar chart in a notebook with seven bars, the aluminium bar far taller than the rest and no bar at all for chips packets.
setup.caption: 2. Draw a bar for each price and compare them.

flow.do: 1. Write seven materials in a list: aluminium, iron and steel, clear plastic bottles, newspaper, cardboard, glass, chips packets. 2. Ask which one a scrap dealer pays most for. 3. Ask which one the dealer will not take at all. 4. Write the guesses and the reasons.
flow.say: A scrap dealer buys waste by the kilogram. Which of these do you think earns the most for one kilogram? Which earns nothing? Why?
flow.kid: Write the seven materials in a list. Which one earns the most for one kilogram? Which earns nothing? Say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Scrap Price Chart. Here you guess which waste material a scrap dealer pays most for.

flow.do: 1. Go with your child to a scrap dealer, or ask the kabadiwala who comes to your street. 2. Ask the price of 1 kilogram of each material. 3. Write each price beside its name. 4. Ask why some things are not bought at all.
flow.say: Let's ask the person who knows. Ask the price for one kilogram of each thing, and write it down.
flow.kid: Go with a grown-up to a scrap dealer. Ask the price of one kilogram of each material. Write each price down.
flow.parent: If you cannot ask anyone, use these example prices for 1 kilogram. Aluminium is 100 rupees, iron and steel are 25, clear plastic bottles are 15, and newspaper is 12. Cardboard is 6, glass is 2, and chips packets are worth nothing. Real prices change by city and by month.
flow.context: This step of The Scrap Price Chart collects the prices. You ask a scrap dealer what one kilogram of each material sells for.

flow.do: 1. Draw a bar chart with one bar for each material. 2. Use 1 centimetre for every 10 rupees. 3. Ask why aluminium is worth so much. 4. Ask why nobody buys chips packets.
flow.say: Draw a bar for each price. Now look at the tallest bar and the missing bar. Why is one worth so much and one worth nothing?
flow.kid: Draw a bar for each price. Find the tallest bar. Find the missing bar. Say why they are so different.

ask.q: Why is aluminium worth so much?
good: Making new aluminium from ore takes a great deal of electricity. Melting old aluminium takes very little.
It can be remelted again and again and stays as good.

ask.q: Why does nobody buy chips packets?
good: They are layers of plastic and metal stuck together, so no factory can use them as one material.
They are so light that a kilogram would need hundreds of packets.

check.q: A scrap dealer pays a lot for aluminium cans and nothing for chips packets. Why?
options: Cans are one material that can be remelted
Packets are dirty and cans are clean
check.why: A can is one metal, and remelting it saves most of the energy of making new metal. A chips packet is plastic and metal stuck together, which no factory can separate cheaply. The price is paid for each kilogram, so the weight of one can does not explain it.

flow.context: This is the last step of The Scrap Price Chart. Here you draw the prices as bars and explain the highest and the lowest.

activities.title: Use Time, Lasting Time
activities.context: In this activity you compare two times for six things you used today: how long you used each one, and how long it will last as waste.

materials.item: six things used today, such as a milk packet, a newspaper, a banana, a toffee and a steel tumbler
a notebook and a pencil

activities.record: Keep the table. Circle the thing with the biggest gap between its use time and its lasting time.

example_chart.title: Rough estimates of how long things last as waste in the open
rows: nobody knows, a very long time
example_chart.note: The times for tin, aluminium and the plastic bottle come from a sea-debris chart by the US National Park Service, Mote Marine Laboratory and NOAA. That chart gives no time for glass. The peel, newspaper and cloth times are rough guesses. All of them change with the place. Nobody has watched a plastic bottle for 450 years, so that number is worked out from short tests.

setup.art: Six things in a row on a table: a milk packet, a newspaper, a banana, a toffee in its wrapper, a plastic bottle and a steel tumbler.
setup.caption: 1. Choose six things you used today.

setup.art: A notebook table with three columns headed 'Thing', 'Used for' and 'Lasts as waste for', partly filled in.
setup.caption: 2. Write how long you used each thing, and how long it lasts as waste.

flow.do: 1. Choose six things used in your home today. 2. Make a table with three columns: Thing, Used for, Lasts as waste for. 3. Write how long each thing was used, from opening it to throwing it. 4. For a thing that is not thrown, such as a steel tumbler, write 'still in use'.
flow.say: How long did we use each of these? Count from the moment we opened it to the moment we threw it out.
flow.kid: Choose six things you used today. Write how long each one was used. Count from opening it to throwing it.
flow.parent: A milk packet is used for about a day. A toffee wrapper is used for a few minutes, after weeks in the shop. A newspaper is used for a day.
flow.context: This is the first step of Use Time, Lasting Time. Here you write how long six things were used before they were thrown out.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to guess how long each thing will last after it is thrown. 2. Ask for a reason. 3. Write the guesses in pencil in the third column.
flow.say: After we throw each thing out, how long will it go on existing? A week? A year? Longer than you will live? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess how long each thing lasts after it is thrown. A week? A year? Longer than your life? Say why. Write your guesses.
flow.context: This step of Use Time, Lasting Time is for guessing. You guess how long each thing goes on existing after it is thrown out.

flow.do: 1. Show the table of rough estimates. 2. Write the estimate beside each guess. 3. For each thing, work out how many times longer it lasts than it was used. 4. Use days for both numbers. Count a year as 365 days.
flow.say: Here are scientists' rough estimates. Write them in. Now work out how many times longer each thing lasts than we used it.
flow.kid: Write the estimate beside each guess. Change both times into days. Divide the lasting time by the use time.
flow.parent: A peel used for 1 day lasts about 30 days, which is 30 times longer. A plastic bottle used for 1 day lasts about 450 years. That is 450 × 365 = 164,250 days, so 164,250 times longer.
flow.context: This step of Use Time, Lasting Time does the sums. You work out how many times longer each thing lasts than it was used.

flow.do: 1. Circle the thing with the biggest gap. 2. Ask what could do the same job with a smaller gap. 3. Ask which thing has no gap at all.
flow.say: Which thing has the biggest gap between its use and its lasting? What could do the same job and not last so long?
flow.kid: Circle the thing with the biggest gap. What could do the same job with a smaller gap? Which thing has no gap?

ask.q: Which thing has no gap at all?
good: The steel tumbler, because it is still in use. It lasts a long time and is used for a long time.

check.q: Which thing lasts the longest as waste, compared with how long it is used?
options: A banana peel from one snack
A plastic bottle used for one day
A steel tumbler used for twenty years
A newspaper read for one day
check.why: The bottle is used for a day and lasts for hundreds of years. The peel and the newspaper rot within weeks. The tumbler lasts long, but it is used for all that time. Choosing the tumbler means looking only at how long a thing lasts.

flow.context: This is the last step of Use Time, Lasting Time. Here you find the thing that lasts longest compared with its use.

activities.title: Breaks Up, Not Away: a paper model of microplastic
activities.context: In this activity a square of paper stands for a plastic bag lying in the sun. You cut it in half again and again. This shows what happens to the amount of plastic when a bag cracks into pieces.

materials.item: a square of coloured paper, 16 centimetres on each side
scissors
a large steel plate or tray
a small piece of thermocol from old packing, if you have one
a damp paper napkin

activities.record: Write the number of pieces after each round of cutting. Write one sentence saying what happened to the total amount of paper.

setup.art: A square of coloured paper cut into two halves, then four quarters, with scissors beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Cut the square in half. Then cut every piece in half again.

setup.art: Sixty-four small paper pieces pushed together on a tray to rebuild the outline of the first square.
setup.caption: 2. After six rounds, push all the pieces back together. Is any paper missing?

setup.art: A child's fingers rubbing a small piece of thermocol over a steel plate covered in tiny white beads.
setup.caption: 3. Rub a piece of thermocol over a plate and look at the beads.

flow.do: 1. Show the paper square and say it stands for a plastic bag in the sun. 2. Explain that sunlight makes plastic brittle, so it cracks. 3. Ask whether there is less plastic after a bag has cracked into tiny pieces. 4. Ask for the reason.
flow.say: Sunlight makes a plastic bag brittle, and it cracks into pieces. After many years of cracking, is there less plastic than before? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: This paper stands for a plastic bag. Sunlight cracks a bag into pieces. Is there less plastic afterwards? Say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of Breaks Up, Not Away. Here you guess whether a cracked plastic bag is less plastic than a whole one.

flow.do: 1. Cut the square in half. That is round 1, and there are 2 pieces. 2. Cut every piece in half. That is round 2. 3. Keep going for 6 rounds, working over the plate. 4. Write the number of pieces after each round. 5. Push all the pieces together to rebuild the square.
flow.say: Cut every piece in half, and count the pieces after each round. After six rounds, try to build the square again.
flow.kid: Cut the square in half. Cut every piece in half again. Do 6 rounds. Count the pieces each time. Then rebuild the square.
flow.parent: The pieces go 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64. Rebuilt, they cover the same square as before. Nothing has gone. There are only more pieces, and each is smaller.
flow.context: This is the main step of Breaks Up, Not Away. Here you cut a paper square in half six times and count the pieces.

flow.do: 1. Hold the thermocol over the plate and rub it gently with a thumb. 2. Look at the white beads that fall. 3. Try to pick up every bead. 4. Wipe the plate with the damp napkin and put the napkin in the dry waste.
flow.say: This is real plastic. Rub it gently and look at what falls. Can you pick every bead up again?
flow.kid: Rub the thermocol gently over the plate. Look at the beads. Try to pick up every one. Wipe the plate with the damp napkin.
flow.parent: Skip this step if you have no thermocol. Keep the beads on the plate, because they blow about easily. The damp napkin picks them up.
flow.context: This step of Breaks Up, Not Away uses real plastic. You rub a piece of thermocol and see how easily it breaks into beads.

flow.do: 1. Ask what happened to the amount of paper. 2. Ask what the model says about a plastic bag in a field. 3. Ask what is different about real plastic pieces.
flow.say: What happened to the number of pieces? What happened to the total amount of paper? What does that tell us about a plastic bag in a field?
flow.kid: What happened to the number of pieces? What happened to the total amount? What does that say about a plastic bag?

ask.q: What is harder about many tiny pieces than one big piece?
good: They cannot be picked up again.
Small animals and fish can swallow them.
Wind and water carry them everywhere.

check.q: A plastic bag in a field cracks into thousands of tiny pieces. What has happened to the plastic?
options: There is the same amount, in smaller pieces
There is less plastic than before
check.why: Cracking only makes the pieces smaller. Put together, they would make the same bag. Choosing 'rotted' mixes up breaking up, which sunlight does, with breaking down, which only decomposers can do.

flow.context: This is the last step of Breaks Up, Not Away. Here you say what the paper model shows about plastic that cracks into pieces.

activities.title: Where Did the Peel Go? Follow one banana peel four ways
activities.context: In this activity you draw what happens to the matter in one banana peel in four places: a compost pot, deep in a dump, a street fire and a cow's stomach.

materials.item: a large sheet of paper
a pencil and colour pencils

activities.record: Keep the drawing. Under it, write one sentence that is true of all four boxes.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a banana peel drawn in the middle and four empty boxes round it labelled 'compost pot', 'deep in a dump', 'street fire' and 'cow'.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a peel in the middle and four boxes round it.

setup.art: The same sheet with coloured arrows leading out of each box to the words 'air', 'soil', 'water' and 'a living body'.
setup.caption: 2. In each box, draw arrows to show where the peel's matter goes.

flow.do: 1. Draw a banana peel in the middle of the paper. 2. Draw four boxes round it and label them: COMPOST POT, DEEP IN A DUMP, STREET FIRE, COW. 3. Ask in which box the peel is most completely gone, and why.
flow.say: One peel could end up in any of these four places. In which place is it most completely gone? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Draw a peel in the middle. Draw four boxes round it. Label them. In which box is the peel most completely gone? Say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of Where Did the Peel Go. Here you draw four places a banana peel could end up, and guess where it is most completely gone.

flow.do: 1. Take one box at a time. 2. Ask who or what changes the peel there. 3. Ask what the peel turns into. 4. Draw an arrow for each thing that leaves, and write where it goes: AIR, SOIL, WATER or A LIVING BODY.
flow.say: Who changes the peel in this box? What does the peel turn into? Draw an arrow for each thing, and write where it goes.
flow.kid: Take one box at a time. Who changes the peel there? What does the peel turn into? Draw an arrow to where each thing goes.
flow.parent: In a compost pot, decomposers work with air. Carbon dioxide and water vapour go to the air, and compost goes to the soil. Deep in a dump, microbes work without air. Methane and carbon dioxide go to the air, and leachate goes to the water under the dump. In a street fire, carbon dioxide, water vapour and smoke go to the air, and ash goes to the soil. A cow uses some of the peel to build her body and her milk. Some leaves in her breath, and the rest leaves as dung, which decomposers eat.
flow.context: This is the main step of Where Did the Peel Go. Here you draw arrows to show where the matter of the peel goes in each of four places.

flow.do: 1. Look at all four boxes together. 2. Ask in which box any of the peel's matter stopped existing. 3. Ask which box does the most good, and which does the most harm.
flow.say: Look at all four boxes. In which one did any of the peel stop existing? Which box does the most good? Which does the most harm?
flow.kid: Look at all four boxes. Did any of the peel stop existing? Which box does the most good? Which does harm?

ask.q: In which box did some of the peel's matter stop existing?
good: In none of them. Every bit went somewhere: the air, the soil, the water or a body.

check.q: A banana peel is burnt in a street fire. Where is most of its matter afterwards?
options: In the ash on the ground
In the air, as gases and smoke
check.why: Burning joins the peel's atoms with oxygen, and most of them leave as carbon dioxide, water vapour and smoke. Only a little ash stays. Choosing 'nowhere' means thinking that what we cannot see has stopped existing.

flow.context: This is the last step of Where Did the Peel Go. Here you compare the four boxes and say whether any matter was destroyed.

projects.title: The Seven-Day Waste Count: what is our family's waste made of?
projects.context: In this seven-day project you weigh your family's waste every evening, kind by kind. At the end you chart it and work out how much each person makes in a day. Then you plan one way to make less.

materials.item: containers or bags for five kinds of waste
a kitchen scale, or a clothes hanger, two carry bags, a 1-litre bottle and a measuring cup
household gloves
a notebook, a pencil and a ruler
soap and water for washing hands

projects.safety: Never open or sort waste that is already mixed. Wear gloves when you lift the wet waste bag, and keep the bag closed. Wash your hands with soap for 20 seconds afterwards. Hazardous waste and sanitary waste are counted, not weighed or handled.

schedule.what: Label five containers. Weigh each one empty. Learn to weigh with the scale or the hanger balance.
In the evening, weigh each container and write the mass of waste.
Weigh each container and write the mass of waste.
Weigh each container and write the mass of waste.
Weigh each container and write the mass of waste.
Weigh each container and write the mass of waste.
Weigh once more. Add up each kind and draw a bar chart. Find the waste for each person in a day, and choose one kind to cut.

projects.record: Keep the daily table, the bar chart and a half-page report. The report says which kind of waste was heaviest and how much each person makes in a day. It also says what the family will change.

setup.art: Five containers in a kitchen corner labelled WET, PAPER AND CARD, PLASTIC THAT SELLS, PACKETS AND WRAPPERS, and GLASS AND METAL.
setup.caption: 1. Set up five labelled containers and weigh each one empty.

setup.art: A clothes hanger hung on a door hook with a closed bag of waste on one end and a bottle partly filled with water on the other, hanging level.
setup.caption: 2. Each evening, weigh each kind of waste. Water in a bottle can be the weight.

setup.art: A notebook with a table of seven days and five kinds of waste, and below it a bar chart with the 'WET' bar the tallest.
setup.caption: 3. On day 7, add up each kind and draw a bar chart.

flow.do: 1. Label five containers: WET, PAPER AND CARD, PLASTIC THAT SELLS, PACKETS AND WRAPPERS, GLASS AND METAL. 2. Weigh each empty container and write its mass on its label. 3. With no scale, hang a hanger on a hook with a carry bag on each end. 4. Put the thing to be weighed in one bag and a bottle in the other. 5. Pour water into the bottle from the measuring cup until the hanger is level. 6. Each millilitre of water is 1 gram.
flow.say: For seven days, every bit of our waste goes into one of these five. Each evening we weigh them. What do you think will be heaviest? Why?
flow.kid: Label five containers. Weigh each one empty. Write its mass on the label. Guess which kind of waste will be heaviest. Say why.

ask.q: Which kind of waste do you think will be heaviest by the end of the week? Why?
good: Wet waste, because peels and leftovers are full of water.
Plastic, because we see so much of it. (A fair guess. The count will show.)

flow.parent: PLASTIC THAT SELLS means bottles, rinsed milk packets and hard plastic. PACKETS AND WRAPPERS means chips packets, sachets and wrappers. If you use the hanger scale, the bottle in one bag has a mass of its own. To cancel it out, put an empty bottle of the same kind in the other bag, beside the waste. Keep sanitary waste and hazardous waste out of the count. Just note how many pieces there are.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Seven-Day Waste Count. Here you set up five labelled containers and learn how to weigh them.

flow.do: 1. Each evening, wear gloves and close the wet waste bag. 2. Weigh each container with its waste. 3. Subtract the mass of the empty container. 4. Write the mass of waste in the table. 5. Empty the containers in the usual way and wash your hands with soap. 6. Do this for days 2 to 6, about 5 minutes each evening.
flow.say: Weigh each one, then take away the mass of the empty container. What is left is the mass of the waste.
flow.kid: Each evening, weigh each container. Take away the mass of the empty container. Write the mass of waste. Wash your hands with soap.
flow.wait: Do this every evening from day 2 to day 6.
flow.parent: Subtracting the empty container is called taking the tare. If a day is missed, weigh two days together and write half for each day.
flow.context: This is the daily step of The Seven-Day Waste Count. Each evening you weigh the five kinds of waste and write the masses in a table.

flow.do: 1. On day 7, weigh once more. 2. Add up the seven days for each kind of waste. 3. Add the five totals to get the week's waste. 4. Divide by 7, then by the number of people at home. 5. Draw a bar chart with one bar for each kind.
flow.say: Add up each kind. Which is the tallest bar? Now divide the week's total by seven, and then by the number of us.
flow.kid: Add up each kind of waste. Add the five totals. Divide by 7. Divide by the number of people. Draw a bar for each kind.

ask.q: Which kind was heaviest? Which kind took the most room in the bin?
good: Wet waste was heaviest.
Packets and plastic took the most room, though they weighed little.

flow.parent: In many Indian homes wet waste is about half the mass or more. Studies of Indian cities find a few hundred grams of waste for each person in a day. Your number may be lower or higher.
flow.context: This step of The Seven-Day Waste Count works out the results. You total each kind of waste, find the amount for each person in a day and draw a bar chart.

flow.do: 1. Ask which kind of waste the family could cut most easily. 2. Use the waste hierarchy: first refuse or reduce, then reuse, then recycle or compost. 3. Agree on one change for the next week. 4. Write a half-page report with the chart and the plan.
flow.say: Look at the chart. Which bar could we make shorter next week? What exactly will we do differently?
flow.kid: Look at your chart. Which bar could be shorter next week? Choose one change. Write a half-page report.

ask.q: Which change comes highest on the waste hierarchy?
good: Not buying the thing at all, such as carrying a bottle of water from home.
Buying loose snacks in our own box, so there is no packet.

check.q: A bin with waste weighs 1,350 grams. The empty bin weighs 400 grams. What is the mass of the waste?
check.why: Take the empty bin away from the full bin: 1,350 − 400 = 950 grams. Choosing 1,350 means counting the bin as waste. Choosing 1,750 means adding where you should subtract.

flow.context: This is the last step of The Seven-Day Waste Count. Here you choose one kind of waste to cut and write a short report.

challenges.title: A Dump That Does Not Leak
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. Rain that soaks through a dump comes out as dirty water, called leachate. Here you build a small model dump, and design a liner that keeps its leachate from reaching the ground.
challenges.problem: Build a model dump that holds 100 millilitres of 'rain' for 10 minutes without one drop leaking out below. Then find a way to take the dirty water out.
constraints: The 'waste' is 2 tablespoons of today's used tea leaves, cooled. Add a pinch of turmeric and a pinch of salt.
The dump is the top half of a plastic bottle, turned upside down with the cap off. It stands in a glass tumbler.
The liner may use newspaper, cloth, a piece of carry bag, or kneaded atta dough, which stands for clay.
Pour the 100 millilitres slowly, over about one minute.
materials: a plastic bottle cut in half by a grown-up
used tea leaves, turmeric and salt
newspaper, a cotton rag and a piece of plastic carry bag
a lump of kneaded atta dough the size of a lemon
a drinking straw or a spoon
a measuring cup and a watch
challenges.safety: A grown-up cuts the bottle and covers the cut edge with tape. Use only fresh, cooled tea leaves. Put them in the wet waste afterwards and wash your hands with soap.
general: Line the funnel with a piece of plastic carry bag, pressed well into the neck.
Use two layers, so that a hole in one is covered by the other.
Press atta dough into the neck as a plug of 'clay'.
creative: Put dough under the plastic sheet, so that a pinhole in the plastic still does not leak. Real landfills use clay under plastic for this reason.
Slope the liner so that the dirty water runs to one low corner. Lift it out with a straw, holding a finger over the top end.
Add a 'roof' over the waste so that less rain gets in. Real landfills are covered with soil and a cap when they are full.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own liner. Draw it first and label each layer. Build it, pour the rain and time 10 minutes. Then make one pinhole in your plastic layer and test again. Does your design still hold?

setup.art: The top half of a plastic bottle turned upside down in a glass tumbler like a funnel, with wet tea leaves inside and yellow-brown water dripping into the tumbler.
setup.caption: 1. With no liner, pour rain on the 'waste' and watch what drips out.

setup.art: The same funnel lined with a layer of dough and a piece of plastic bag, tea leaves on top, and a dry tumbler underneath.
setup.caption: 2. Build a liner and test whether it holds the rain for 10 minutes.

setup.art: A child lifting dirty water out of the lined funnel with a straw, a finger pressed over the straw's top end.
setup.caption: 3. Find a way to take the dirty water out.

flow.do: 1. Stand the bottle top upside down in a tumbler, with the cap off. 2. Mix the tea leaves, turmeric and salt and put them in the funnel. 3. Ask what will come out when it rains on this dump, and why. 4. Pour 100 millilitres of water slowly over the waste. 5. Look at the water in the tumbler.
flow.say: This is a dump with nothing under it. If rain falls on it, what will come out at the bottom? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Put the tea leaf 'waste' in the funnel. Guess what will drip out when it rains. Say why. Pour the water slowly. Look in the tumbler.
flow.parent: Yellow-brown water runs into the tumbler. It carries colour from the tea and turmeric, and salt that cannot be seen. This is leachate. Do not taste it.
flow.context: This is the first step of A Dump That Does Not Leak. Here you pour water on a model dump with no liner and see the leachate come out.

flow.do: 1. Empty and rinse the funnel and the tumbler. 2. Ask your child to draw a liner design and label the layers. 3. Build the liner inside the funnel. 4. Put fresh tea leaf 'waste' on top of the liner.
flow.say: Now you are the engineer. What will you put under the waste, so that no dirty water reaches the tumbler? Why that?
flow.kid: Rinse the funnel. Draw your liner and label each layer. Build it inside the funnel. Put new 'waste' on top.
flow.parent: Newspaper and cloth soak through within a minute. Plastic holds unless there is a gap at its edge. Dough holds well if it is pressed against the sides all the way round.
flow.context: This step of A Dump That Does Not Leak is for designing. You draw a liner, build it in the funnel and put the waste on top.

flow.do: 1. Stand the funnel in a clean, dry tumbler. 2. Pour 100 millilitres of water slowly over the waste. 3. Time 10 minutes and count any drops that fall. 4. If it leaks, find where, mend the design and test again.
flow.say: Pour the rain slowly. Now we wait ten minutes and count every drop. If it leaks, where is the water getting through?
flow.kid: Stand the funnel in a dry tumbler. Pour the rain slowly. Wait 10 minutes. Count the drops. If it leaks, mend it and test again.

ask.q: If your liner leaked, where did the water get through?
good: At the edge, where the plastic did not reach the side.
Through the newspaper, because paper soaks up water.

flow.context: This step of A Dump That Does Not Leak is the test. You pour water on your lined dump and count the drops that leak in 10 minutes.

flow.do: 1. Look inside the funnel. The dirty water is now sitting in the dump. 2. Ask what should be done with it. 3. Try to take it out with a straw or a spoon, without moving the waste. 4. Compare your model with a real landfill.
flow.say: Your liner held. But where is the dirty water now? It has not gone. What would you do with it in a real landfill?
flow.kid: Look inside the funnel. Where is the dirty water now? Try to take it out with a straw. What would a real landfill do?
flow.parent: A real landfill has pipes at the bottom that carry the leachate to a tank, where it is cleaned. A liner without pipes fills up like a bathtub and overflows.

check.q: A landfill has a perfect liner but no pipes. It rains for years. What happens to the leachate?
options: It dries up inside the waste
It collects until it overflows the liner
check.why: The liner stops the leachate going down, so it collects inside like water in a tub. It must be piped out and cleaned. Choosing 'dries up' forgets that more rain keeps coming.

flow.context: This is the last step of A Dump That Does Not Leak. Here you find that the dirty water is still inside the dump, and work out how to remove it.

challenges.title: The One-Material Pack: keep a snack crisp for two days
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. In Scrunch and Peel, a chips packet turned out to be plastic and metal stuck together, which nobody can recycle. Here you design a pack that keeps a snack crisp. Every part of it must rot, be reused or be recycled.
challenges.problem: Design and build a pack that keeps four pieces of roasted papad crisp for two days. Every part of the pack must be a single material that rots, can be reused or can be recycled.
constraints: No part may be two materials stuck together.
Test against two controls: papad left open on a plate, and papad in an old chips packet closed with a clip.
After two days, a papad piece passes if it still snaps cleanly when you bend it.
Write down what happens to each part of your pack after the snack is eaten.
materials: one roasted papad broken into 12 pieces
a steel box or a glass jar with a lid
newspaper, butter paper or a brown paper bag
a banana leaf, a dry leaf plate or a cotton cloth
an empty chips packet and a clip, for the control
general: Use a steel box with a tight lid, which can be used for many years.
Use a glass jar with a screw lid.
Wrap the papad in paper and tie it with string. This is easy to make, but paper lets damp air through.
creative: Wrap in paper for the shop shelf, and sell it inside a tin that the shop takes back and refills.
Put a spoon of dry rice in a cloth pouch inside the box, to soak up damp.
Make the pack thicker with many layers of one material, such as paper, and test how many layers are needed.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own pack. Draw it and name the material of every part. Build it, test it against the two controls for two days, and write what you found. Then say honestly what the chips packet did better.

setup.art: Twelve pieces of roasted papad on a plate beside a steel box, a glass jar, sheets of paper, a banana leaf and string.
setup.caption: 1. Break a roasted papad into 12 pieces and choose your materials.

setup.art: Three things in a row on a shelf: an open plate with papad, a clipped chips packet, and a child's own pack tied with string.
setup.caption: 2. Put 4 pieces in your pack, 4 on an open plate and 4 in an old chips packet.

setup.art: A child bending a piece of papad that snaps cleanly in two, with a notebook table beside it.
setup.caption: 3. After two days, bend a piece from each. Does it still snap?

flow.do: 1. Look at an empty chips packet together. 2. Ask what jobs the packet does for the snack. 3. Ask what happens to the packet afterwards. 4. Read the problem and the rules aloud.
flow.say: A chips packet does several jobs very well. What are they? And what happens to the packet when the chips are finished?
flow.kid: Look at an empty chips packet. What jobs does it do for the snack? What happens to it afterwards? Read the problem.

ask.q: What jobs does the packet do?
good: It keeps damp air out, so the snack stays crisp.
It keeps light out and stops the snack being crushed.
It is very light and very cheap.

flow.parent: Be fair to the packet. It weighs only a few grams and keeps food fresh for months. That is why companies use it. The cost comes afterwards, because nobody can recycle it.
flow.context: This is the first step of The One-Material Pack. Here you work out what jobs a chips packet does, before you design a better one.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to draw a pack and name the material of each part. 2. Check that no part is two materials stuck together. 3. Build the pack. 4. Put 4 papad pieces in it, 4 on an open plate and 4 in a clipped chips packet. 5. Put all three on the same shelf.
flow.say: Draw your pack first, and tell me what each part is made of. Then build it. All three go on the same shelf, so the test is fair.
flow.kid: Draw your pack. Name the material of each part. Build it. Put 4 pieces in it. Put 4 on a plate and 4 in a chips packet.
flow.context: This step of The One-Material Pack is for building. You design and make a pack from single materials, and set up two controls beside it.

flow.do: 1. After two days, take one piece from each of the three. 2. Bend each piece and listen. 3. Write 'snaps' or 'bends' for each. 4. Taste one piece from each, if it was kept clean.
flow.say: Bend one piece from each. Does it snap, or does it bend like cloth? Which pack did best?
flow.kid: Take one piece from each. Bend it. Does it snap or bend? Write what you find. Which pack did best?
flow.wait: Leave the three packs on the shelf for 2 days.
flow.parent: In damp weather, the papad on the open plate goes soft within a day. A tight steel box or glass jar usually matches the chips packet. A paper wrap usually does not.
flow.context: This step of The One-Material Pack is the test. After two days you bend a papad piece from each pack to see which stayed crisp.

flow.do: 1. For each part of the pack, ask what happens to it next: rot, reuse or recycle. 2. Ask what the chips packet does better than your child's pack. 3. Ask who would have to change for the new pack to be used: the company, the shop or the buyer.
flow.say: What happens to each part of your pack now? What does the chips packet still do better than yours? Who would have to change to use your pack?
flow.kid: Say what happens to each part of your pack next. What does the chips packet do better? Who would have to change?

ask.q: What does the chips packet still do better?
good: It is lighter, so a lorry can carry more.
It is cheaper, and it needs nobody to bring it back.
It keeps food for months, and mine was tested for two days.

check.q: A steel box keeps a snack as crisp as a chips packet. What is the main cost of using it?
options: The box is heavy and must be brought back
check.why: A steel box lasts for years and can be recycled. But it is heavy, and someone must carry it back to be refilled. The chips packet needs none of that. Every packaging choice gives up something.

flow.context: This is the last step of The One-Material Pack. Here you judge your pack honestly against the chips packet.

items.p: What makes a piece of waste 'organic'?
opts: It came from a living being
items.why: Organic waste was made by a plant or an animal, so decomposers can eat it. Choosing 'wet' is a common slip. Paper and cotton are dry and still organic.

items.p: True or false: newspaper is organic waste, although it is dry.
items.why: True. Paper is made from trees, so decomposers can eat it. A strong answer adds that dry paper still goes in the dry waste, to be recycled first.

items.p: The dirty liquid that drains out of a heap of waste is called ____.
a: leachate
items.why: Rain soaks through the waste and carries dissolved matter with it. Under an open dump, leachate can reach the groundwater.

items.p: Sort these into organic waste and inorganic waste.
items.a: see items
items.why: Tea leaves, cotton, dry leaves and newspaper were made by plants. Glass, steel, foil and tile were made from sand, ore and clay.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These five words are needed to talk about where waste goes. A strong answer could give an example of each.
pairs: Segregation
keeping kinds of waste apart
Compost
what decomposers leave when they have air
Methane
a gas made when waste rots without air
Landfill
a lined place built for burying waste
Recycling
making new things from old material

items.p: A piece of drink bottle sinks in water. A piece of its cap floats. Why?
items.why: The bottle and the cap are different materials. Bottle plastic is denser than water, and cap plastic is less dense. Colour and size make no difference to floating.

items.p: In the Float Tank Test, water sorted 20 mixed flakes. Explain how, using the word 'density'.
items.a: The bottle flakes are denser than water, so they sank. The box flakes are less dense than water, so they floated. I skimmed the floating flakes off the top, and the two plastics were apart.
items.why: A strong answer says which plastic is denser than water and which is less dense, and how that separated them.

items.p: Draw a lined landfill. Show the liner, the waste, the soil cover and a pipe for leachate.
items.a: A pit with a liner along the bottom and sides, layers of waste inside and soil on top. A pipe at the lowest point leads to a tank.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the liner under all the waste and the pipe at the lowest point, where leachate collects.
items.art: A blank box for a drawing.

items.p: Three of these can be melted and remade again and again. Which is the odd one out?
items.why: Glass, aluminium and steel are single materials that can be remelted without end. A chips packet is plastic and metal stuck together, so no factory can remelt it.

items.p: True or false: burning a heap of dry leaves destroys the matter in them.
items.why: False. The matter leaves as carbon dioxide, water vapour and smoke, and a little stays as ash. No atom is destroyed.

items.p: Put the waste hierarchy in order, with the best choice first.
a: Refuse or reduce
Reuse
Recycle
Recover, as compost or biogas
Dispose in a landfill
items.why: The earlier the step, the less matter has to be moved, melted or stored. Refusing makes no waste at all.

items.p: The number in the small triangle on a plastic thing is called the resin ____.
a: code
items.why: The resin code names the kind of plastic, from 1 to 7. It is not a promise that the thing will be recycled.

items.p: A family has a big heap of dry leaves swept from the yard. Two neighbours disagree about it.
items.a: A strong answer says that burning moves the leaves into the air as smoke and gases, which everyone breathes. It also takes the other side seriously: a loose heap can shelter pests, so the leaves should go in a covered compost pit or bin.
items.why: Both neighbours want a clean, safe yard. The science shows where the leaves go in each plan.

views.says: Burn them. It takes two minutes, and a leaf heap brings mosquitoes and hides snakes.
Let them rot in a corner. Smoke hurts our lungs, and rotted leaves feed the plants.

items.ask: Which neighbour do you agree with? Use what you know about where burnt matter goes. Then say one thing the other neighbour has right.

items.p: Which of these is hazardous waste?
items.why: A battery holds metals that can leak and poison soil and water. The other three are ordinary wet or dry waste.

items.p: Rain falls on an open dump for many years. Explain how this can spoil a well nearby.
items.a: Rainwater soaks down through the waste and picks up salts, rotting matter and metals. This leachate seeps into the soil under the dump and reaches the groundwater. The well draws from that groundwater.
items.why: A strong answer follows the water step by step: rain, through the waste, into the soil, into the groundwater, into the well.

items.p: Deep inside a dump there is no air. Which gas does rotting food make there?
items.why: Without air, a different set of microbes takes over, and they give off methane. Methane burns and traps heat in the air.

items.p: A chips packet springs open after you scrunch it. Kitchen foil stays in a ball. What does this tell you?
items.a: The chips packet is mostly plastic film, which springs back. Kitchen foil is metal, which stays bent. So the silver inside the packet is only a very thin coat of metal on plastic.
items.why: A strong answer uses the result as evidence about the material, and does not judge by the silver colour.

items.p: True or false: a triangle of arrows on a packet means the packet will be recycled.
items.why: False. The number inside only names the kind of plastic. Recycling happens only if someone collects, sorts and buys it.

items.p: A piece of plastic smaller than 5 millimetres is called a ____.
a: microplastic
items.why: Big plastic things crack into microplastics. They are too small to pick up, and they do not rot.

items.p: Sort these by what should be done with each.
items.a: see items
items.why: Organic kitchen waste can be composted. Clean single materials can be sold. Things that poison or cut are kept apart in a closed box.

items.p: Flattened dry waste filled a quarter of the bucket it had filled before. What left the bucket?
items.why: Bottles and boxes are mostly air inside. Flattening pushes the air out. The plastic, the card and their mass all stay.

items.p: Draw one banana peel in a compost pot. Add arrows to show where its matter goes.
items.a: A peel in a pot with decomposers on it. One arrow goes up to the air, labelled carbon dioxide and water vapour. One arrow goes down, labelled compost.
items.why: A strong drawing shows matter going two ways: into the air as gases and into the soil as compost. It shows decomposers doing the work.
items.art: A blank box for a drawing.

items.p: A city's dump is full. The council must decide what to do with the waste. Three people speak.
items.a: A strong answer notes that about half of Indian city waste is wet, which composts well and burns poorly. It may still allow burning for the dry waste that nobody can recycle. It takes the engineer's point seriously: the dump is full and something must be done now.
items.why: This is a real argument in Indian cities. Each speaker has part of the truth, and the evidence about wet waste matters most.

views.says: Build a plant that burns the waste for electricity. Burning shrinks waste to a tenth of its size.
Burning takes the paper and plastic that we sort and sell. Our waste is wet and burns badly.
I worry about the smoke. Filters work only if someone keeps them running.

items.ask: Which plan would you choose for the city? Give evidence. Then say what one of the other speakers has right.

items.p: Food waste is tipped into a small pond. Put what follows in order.
a: Microbes multiply to eat the food
The microbes use up the oxygen in the water
Fish cannot get enough oxygen
Many fish die
items.why: Rotting uses oxygen. In a pond there is only a little oxygen dissolved in the water, and the fish need the same oxygen.
items: Microbes multiply to eat the food
The microbes use up the oxygen in the water

items.p: Leftover food is organic and rots. Explain why it can still do harm in a dump.
items.a: Deep in a dump there is no air. The food rots slowly there and gives off methane, which can start fires and traps heat in the air. The liquid from the rotting food also joins the leachate.
items.why: A strong answer says that the place decides the harm. The same food in a compost pot with air would do good.

items.p: Match each kind of waste to the harm it can do.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each harm comes from what the waste is made of and where it ends up. A strong answer could say how each could be prevented.
pairs: Plastic bags in a street drain
streets flood in heavy rain
Food waste in a pond
fish die for lack of oxygen
A battery in an open dump
metals leak into the groundwater
Plastic burnt in a street fire
poisonous smoke in the air
A plastic bag at an open bin
a cow swallows it with the food

items.p: Paper can be recycled about five to seven times. Why not for ever?
opts: Its fibres get shorter each time
items.why: Each time paper is pulped, its plant fibres break and get shorter. Short fibres cannot hold a sheet together. Glass and metal do not have this limit.

items.p: Three of these are multi-layer packaging. Which is the odd one out?
items.why: A glass jar is one material. The carton, the chips packet and the sachet are thin layers of different materials stuck together.

items.p: Label the four parts of the landfill: the liner, the leachate pipe, the gas pipe and the soil cover.
a: Liner: the layer of clay and plastic under all the waste
Leachate pipe: at the lowest point of the liner
Gas pipe: standing up through the waste
Soil cover: on top of the waste
items.why: Each part stops one harm. The liner and its pipe protect the groundwater. The gas pipe takes the methane out. The cover keeps rain, flies and birds off.
items.art: A cut-away drawing of a landfill with a line along the bottom, a pipe at the lowest point, a pipe rising through the waste and a layer on top, each with a blank label.

items.p: Four people made 4,200 grams of wet waste in 7 days. Find the amount for each person in a day.
items.a: 150 grams. First find one day: 4,200 ÷ 7 = 600 grams. Then share it among 4 people: 600 ÷ 4 = 150 grams.
items.why: A strong answer shows both steps: divide by the days, then by the people.

items.p: People say waste is 'thrown away'. Use what you know about atoms to explain why there is no 'away'.
items.a: Atoms are not destroyed when waste rots, burns or is buried. They only move to the air, the water or the soil, or stay where they are. So every bit of waste is still somewhere on the Earth.
items.why: A strong answer names at least two places where the matter goes, and says that no atom stops existing.

items.p: A snack company sells chips in a packet that nobody can recycle. Three people speak about the empty packets.
items.a: A strong answer uses the finding that a multi-layer packet cannot be separated or remelted. It notes that the buyer did not choose the material. It is fair to the manager: the packet really does save food and fuel.
items.why: India's rules now make companies collect their plastic back, but people still argue about how well this works.

views.says: Our packet keeps chips fresh for months with three grams of material. Buyers should put it in a bin.
We cannot recycle it. The company chose this packet, so the company should pay to collect it.
I would bring my own box if shops sold chips loose. I can only choose from what is on the shelf.

items.ask: Who should deal with the empty packets? Argue for one view with evidence. Then say what another speaker has right.

items.p: A solid piece of plastic sinks in plain water and floats in strong salt water. What does this show?
opts: It is denser than both liquids
It is denser than plain water only
It is less dense than both
items.why: Its density lies between the two. It is a little denser than plain water and less dense than salt water. The salt changes the water, not the plastic.

items.p: A sack holds chopped bottle bits and cap bits, all mixed. Design a way to separate them.
items.a: Tip the bits into a tank of water and stir. The bottle bits are denser than water and sink. The cap bits are less dense and float. Skim off the floating bits and scoop out the sunk ones.
items.why: A strong answer uses density and says which bits go where. It mentions stirring, so that air bubbles do not hold bits up.

items.p: True or false: a well-lined landfill makes waste harmless for ever.
items.why: False. A landfill only stores waste. Its leachate and gas must be piped out and treated for many years after it is full. Liners can also fail.

items.p: About half of Indian city waste is wet. Why is that a problem for a plant that burns waste?
opts: Wet waste is too heavy to lift
items.why: Much of the heat goes into boiling off the water. So the plant needs extra fuel, or dry waste that could have been recycled. Wet waste composts well instead.

items.p: A plastic bottle and a steel tumbler both last hundreds of years. Why is only the bottle a waste problem?
items.a: The tumbler is used for all the years it lasts, so it does not become waste. The bottle is used for a day and then lies as waste for hundreds of years. The problem is the gap between the use time and the lasting time.
items.why: A strong answer compares use time with lasting time for both things, and does not blame lasting alone.

items.p: Recycling a material into a lower-quality thing that is not recycled again is called ____.
a: downcycling
items.why: A clear bottle made into polyester fibre is downcycled. The fibre is not made back into bottles.

items.p: Sort each thing by where most of its matter is one year later.
items.a: see items
items.why: Burning and rotting without air send matter into the air. Compost and ash join the soil. Glass and plastic stay as they are.
items: a peel burnt in a street fire
finished compost dug into a pot
a glass bottle in a lake
a plastic spoon in a field

items.p: A paper bag takes more water and energy to make than a plastic bag. When is paper better?
opts: Always, whatever is done with it
When it is reused several times
items.why: A study in Britain found that a paper bag must be used 3 times to harm the climate less. Paper also rots if it is littered, which plastic does not. So the answer depends on how the bag is used.

items.p: A used battery is thrown on an open dump. Put what follows in order.
a: The steel case rusts open
Metals leak out of the battery
Rain washes the metals down through the waste
The metals reach the groundwater
People draw the water from a well
items.why: Hazardous waste harms through a chain of small steps. Keeping the battery out of the dump breaks the chain at the start.
items: People draw the water from a well
Rain washes the metals down through the waste
Metals leak out of the battery

items.p: Plastic is made from oil, which formed from ancient sea beings. Is plastic waste organic or inorganic? Argue for one.
items.a: Either answer can be strong. Organic: its atoms came from living beings, and chemists call carbon chains organic. Inorganic: no decomposer can eat it, so it behaves like glass and metal in a dump. The better answer says which meaning of the word it is using.
items.why: A strong answer chooses one, gives a reason from the science, and says what the other side has right.

items.p: Match each rule or action in India to what it does.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each rule acts at a different step. A strong answer could say which step of the waste hierarchy each one belongs to.
pairs: Three bins at home
keeps wet, dry and hazardous waste apart
The 2022 ban on some single-use plastic
stops plastic straws and thermocol plates
Companies must collect their packets back
puts the cost on those who chose the packet
Large housing societies compost on site
keeps wet waste out of the dump
Authorised e-waste collectors
recover metals safely from old phones

items.p: Three of these are near the top of the waste hierarchy. Which is the odd one out?
items.why: The first three reduce or reuse, so no waste is made. Burying is disposal, the last step, which gets nothing back.

items.p: Label where a banana peel's matter goes in each place: compost pot, deep dump, fire and cow.
a: Compost pot: into the soil as compost, and into the air
Deep dump: into the air as methane, and into leachate
Street fire: into the air as gases and smoke
Cow: into her body, her breath and her dung
items.why: In none of the four does any matter stop existing. A strong answer names a place for the matter in every box.
items.art: Four boxes round a banana peel, showing a clay pot, a cut-away waste heap, a small fire and a cow, each with a blank label line.

opts: A glass jar and a steel tin
A newspaper and a cotton rag
A milk packet and a bottle
quiz.why: Newspaper is made from trees and cotton from a plant, so decomposers can eat both. They are dry, but organic does not mean wet.

quiz.p: Why can decomposers eat a peel but not a plastic bag?
opts: They have enzymes for what living beings make
quiz.why: Decomposers have had hundreds of millions of years to fit their enzymes to plants and animals. Plastic is new, and its long chains fit almost no enzyme. Softness makes no difference. A hard coconut shell rots.

quiz.p: Peels rot in a compost pot with plenty of air. What do they become?
quiz.why: With air, decomposers turn peels into compost, carbon dioxide and water. Methane and leachate come from rotting without air, as in a dump.

quiz.p: A sheet of paper weighs 5 grams. Its ash weighs far less. Where is the rest?
opts: It was destroyed by the fire
In the air, as gases and smoke
quiz.why: The atoms joined with oxygen and left as carbon dioxide, water vapour and smoke. Choosing 'destroyed' means thinking that matter we cannot see has stopped existing.

quiz.p: Why can a big dump catch fire by itself?
opts: Buried food waste makes methane, which burns
Plastic gets hot in the rain
quiz.why: Deep in a dump there is no air, so rotting food gives off methane. Methane burns easily and can smoulder inside the heap for weeks.

quiz.p: Two plastic flakes look the same. In water, one sinks and one floats. What can you say for sure?
opts: One is older than the other
One is dirtier than the other
quiz.why: The same water treated them differently, so their densities differ, and so they are different materials. Age and dirt do not change whether a plastic floats.

quiz.p: Why does a recycling factory want one kind of plastic at a time?
opts: Mixed plastics melt into a weak material
Mixed plastics rot in the machine
quiz.why: Different plastics melt at different temperatures and do not mix well. The result is cloudy and weak, and few buyers want it.

quiz.p: A juice carton is paper, plastic and metal foil stuck together. Why is it hard to recycle?
opts: The layers cannot be pulled apart cheaply
It is too heavy to carry
quiz.why: Each of the three materials can be recycled alone. Stuck together in thin layers, they need special machines to separate, and few places have them.

quiz.p: Where should a used battery go?
opts: In the dry bag with paper
In a separate closed box for hazardous waste
quiz.why: A battery holds metals that leak into soil and water. It is kept apart and given to a collection point. In the dry bag it can be crushed in the truck.

quiz.p: Four people made 14 kilograms of waste in 7 days. How much is that for each person in a day?
quiz.why: One day: 14 ÷ 7 = 2 kilograms. One person: 2 kilograms ÷ 4 = 500 grams. Choosing 2 kilograms stops after the first step.

quiz.p: Which choice is highest on the waste hierarchy?
opts: Carrying water in a steel bottle
quiz.why: Carrying a steel bottle means no plastic bottle is made or thrown at all. Reducing comes before recycling, because nothing has to be collected or melted.

quiz.p: Which of these do scientists still not know about plastic?
opts: How long it really lasts in nature
quiz.why: Plastic has been in wide use for less than a hundred years, so nobody has watched it for longer. The figures of hundreds of years are worked out from short tests.

applications: Plastic recycling plants wash chopped bottles in long tanks of water. The bottle flakes sink, and the cap and label flakes float off the top.
Scrap yards pull steel out of mixed metal with a large magnet. Aluminium is not magnetic, so it stays behind and is sold apart.
Biogas plants in villages and cities keep wet waste in closed tanks. They collect the methane for cooking, for electricity and for buses.
Engineers build landfills with a liner of clay and plastic, and with pipes. The pipes take out the leachate and the methane to be treated.
Large housing societies in Indian cities compost their own wet waste, and use the compost in their gardens.
Authorised e-waste recyclers take old phones apart and recover copper, silver and gold from them.
Some shops sell oil, grains and soap loose, into the buyer's own container. No packet is made at all.

open_questions.q: How long does plastic really last in nature?
open_questions.why_open: Plastic has been in wide use for less than a hundred years, so nobody has watched it for longer. The figures of hundreds of years come from short tests, and plastics differ.

open_questions.q: Can microbes or enzymes be found, or made, that eat plastic fast enough to matter?
open_questions.why_open: In 2016 scientists in Japan found a bacterium that slowly eats the plastic of drink bottles. Others are building faster enzymes. Nobody knows yet whether this can work for whole cities, or for other plastics.

open_questions.q: What do microplastics do inside a human body?
open_questions.why_open: Microplastics have been found in human blood and other parts of the body. Scientists do not yet know how much harm they do, because the studies are new and hard to do.

open_questions.q: What should be done with multi-layer packets?
open_questions.why_open: They save food and fuel, but they cannot be recycled cheaply. Engineers are testing packets made of one plastic only, and ways to dissolve the layers apart. No answer is in wide use yet.

open_questions.q: Who will clean up the waste that is already circling the Earth?
open_questions.why_open: Tens of thousands of pieces of old rockets and dead satellites orbit the Earth. A few test missions have tried to catch one. Nobody has agreed who should pay.

Which thing in our kitchen has never been waste, though it is older than you?
A chips packet is shiny inside. Is it metal? How could we find out?
What would a shop look like if it sold nothing in packets?

jokes.a: It was ready to turn over a new leaf.

jokes.j: What did the bottle say to its cap in the float tank?
jokes.a: You go up, I'll go down. See you at the factory.

jokes.j: Why did the chips packet fail the scrunch test?
Why did the old dump go to the doctor?

maths.problem: The table shows a family's wet waste on 7 days. What is the total, and what is the average for one day?
maths.answer: The total is 5,600 grams. The average is 800 grams a day.
maths.explain: Add the seven days: 750 + 900 + 650 + 800 + 1,100 + 700 + 700 = 5,600 grams. Divide by 7 days: 5,600 ÷ 7 = 800 grams.
maths.context: This is about The Seven-Day Waste Count. There you weigh each kind of your family's waste every evening. These are made-up results.

chart.title: Made-up example results: wet waste each day

maths.why_maths: One day's waste depends on what was cooked that day. An average over seven days gives a number you can plan with.

maths.problem: The bar chart shows one family's waste in a week, in grams. What percentage of the total is wet waste?
maths.explain: Add the five kinds: 5,600 + 1,400 + 700 + 300 + 2,000 = 10,000 grams. Wet waste is 5,600 out of 10,000. Divide both by 100: 56 out of 100, which is 56 percent.
maths.context: This is about The Seven-Day Waste Count. There you total each kind of waste for a week and draw a bar chart. These are made-up results.

chart.title: Made-up example results: one family's waste in a week

maths.why_maths: A percentage shows at once that more than half of this family's waste could be composted.

maths.problem: A city has 1,000,000 people. Each person makes 400 grams of waste a day. How many tonnes is that in a day? A truck carries 8 tonnes. How many truckloads?
maths.answer: 400 tonnes a day, which is 50 truckloads.
maths.explain: 1,000,000 × 400 grams = 400,000,000 grams. There are 1,000 grams in a kilogram, so that is 400,000 kilograms. There are 1,000 kilograms in a tonne, so that is 400 tonnes. 400 ÷ 8 = 50 truckloads.
maths.context: This is about The Seven-Day Waste Count. There you find how much waste each person in your family makes in a day. Here the same sum is done for a whole city.
maths.why_maths: One person's 400 grams looks small. Multiplying by a city shows why a dump grows into a hill.

maths.problem: In the Crush Test, loose waste came up to 28 cm in the bucket. Flattened, it came up to 7 cm. A truck carries the loose dry waste of 500 homes. How many homes' flattened waste could it carry?
maths.explain: 28 ÷ 7 = 4, so the flattened waste takes a quarter of the space. The truck can hold 4 times as much waste: 500 × 4 = 2,000 homes.
maths.context: This is about the Crush Test. There you measure the height of dry waste in a bucket before and after flattening it. These are made-up results.
maths.why_maths: The ratio from one bucket predicts what would happen in a truck, which you cannot test at home.

maths.problem: In Breaks Up, Not Away, the pieces doubled each round: 2, 4, 8. How many pieces are there after 10 rounds? The square was 16 cm by 16 cm. What is the area of each piece then?
maths.answer: 1,024 pieces, each of a quarter of a square centimetre.
maths.explain: Keep doubling: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1,024. The square's area is 16 × 16 = 256 square centimetres. 256 ÷ 1,024 = 0.25 square centimetres. The total area is still 256.
maths.context: This is about Breaks Up, Not Away. There a paper square stands for a plastic bag, and is cut in half again and again.
maths.why_maths: The pattern shows how fast the pieces multiply while the total stays the same. That is how one bag becomes thousands of microplastics.

maths.problem: A scrap dealer pays 12 rupees for 1 kg of newspaper and 100 rupees for 1 kg of aluminium. Which earns more: 3 kg of newspaper or half a kilogram of aluminium cans?
maths.explain: Newspaper: 3 × 12 = 36 rupees. Aluminium: half of 100 = 50 rupees. 50 − 36 = 14 rupees more for the cans, though they weigh one sixth as much.
maths.context: This is about The Scrap Price Chart. There you find what a scrap dealer pays for one kilogram of each material. These are example prices.
maths.why_maths: Working out the money shows which materials are worth collecting, and why some are left on the street.

maths.problem: A peel is used for 1 day and lasts about 30 days as waste. A plastic bottle is used for 1 day and lasts about 450 years. How many times longer than the peel does the bottle last?
maths.explain: Change the years to days: 450 × 365 = 164,250 days. Divide by the peel's 30 days: 164,250 ÷ 30 = 5,475.
maths.context: This is about Use Time, Lasting Time. There you compare how long a thing is used with how long it lasts as waste. The lasting times are rough estimates.
maths.why_maths: Both things were used for the same single day. Comparing their lasting times shows how different their waste is.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people learn that buried waste does not stay where it is put? This card tells the true story, and the idea that turned out wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: In the 1940s, a chemical company in Niagara Falls, in the United States, needed somewhere to put its waste. It tipped more than 20,000 tons of chemicals into an old, unfinished canal called Love Canal. In 1953 it covered the canal with clay and soil. People believed that waste buried under clay would stay where it was put. The land was sold for one dollar, and a school and houses were built on it. In the 1970s, after years of heavy rain and snow, the buried chemicals rose. Dark, oily liquid seeped into basements and gardens. Lois Gibbs lived there, and her young son kept falling ill. In 1978 she went from door to door and asked each family about their health. Beverly Paigen, a scientist, helped her mark the answers on a map. The illnesses lay along old stream beds that ran out from the canal, where water had carried the chemicals. Officials first dismissed the survey. Later the government moved more than 900 families away. In 1980 the United States passed a law that makes companies pay to clean up old dumps.
how_we_found_out.who: Lois Gibbs, a mother with no training in science, and Beverly Paigen, a cancer scientist who helped her
how_we_found_out.when: The waste was buried from 1942 to the early 1950s. The door-to-door survey was made in 1978, and the clean-up law was passed in 1980.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That waste buried under a cover of clay stays where it is put. Rain and groundwater moved the chemicals out along old stream beds. A map of who fell ill showed where they had gone.
how_we_found_out.art: A woman with a clipboard at the front door of a small wooden house, talking to a neighbour, with a fenced-off field and a boarded-up school behind them.

roots.context: We have learned where waste goes and why plastics must be sorted kind by kind. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Float Tank Test, a bottle piece sank and a cap piece floated in the same water. Both were clean, hard plastic, so 'plastic' is a name for many different materials. Melted together, different plastics make a weak material that few factories will buy. So plastic becomes recyclable only when someone has sorted it, kind by kind.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'plastic' as if it were one material, and 'dry waste' as if it were one heap. We also read the small triangle on a packet as a promise that it will be recycled. The triangle only names the kind of plastic. Whether a thing is recyclable depends on the work of sorting, and on who does that work.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Float Tank Test, pieces marked 1 sank and pieces marked 2, 4 and 5 floated. Water sorted twenty look-alike flakes in under a minute, which eyes could not do. Of all the plastic made up to 2015, only about 9 kilograms in every 100 were ever recycled.

three.who_am_i: Your body is built from atoms that were once in peels, leaves and other bodies. One day those atoms will be part of someone else.
three.what_is_life: Living beings pass their materials round. For almost everything that living beings make, there is a decomposer that can eat it. For most of what factories make, there is not.
three.what_is_this_world: The Earth keeps the same atoms. Nothing you throw out leaves the world. It only changes its place and its form.

roots.thread: The Earth has one stock of atoms, and everything is made from it. The same carbon atoms have been air, leaf, peel, soil and child, many times over. Plastic is made of that carbon too, taken from sea beings who died millions of years ago. So a banana peel and a milk packet are made from the same stock of atoms, joined in two different ways. Decomposers can take the peel apart. For most plastics, almost no living being can yet do the same.

teachings.source: Thich Nhat Hanh, in his teaching on roses and garbage, found in several of his books
teachings.teaching: Look deeply at a rose and you see the garbage that the rose will become in a few days. Look deeply at garbage and you see a rose that it can become. A good gardener is not afraid of garbage, because she knows how to turn it into compost.
teachings.link: This is what a compost pot does. In about two months, decomposers turn peels into food for a plant. The teaching fits organic waste well. It does not fit a chips packet, which no gardener can turn into a rose.

teachings.teaching: What is not real never comes to be, and what is real never stops being.
teachings.link: The Gita says this about the self, not about waste. Science found something like it about matter: the atoms in waste never stop existing. They only move and join in new ways.

teachings.teaching: Everything in this moving world belongs to the whole. Enjoy what you are given by letting go, and do not grab what is another's.
teachings.link: The first step of the waste hierarchy is to take less. The Earth's materials are shared with every other being, and what we take and throw stays in their world too.

science.text: Matter is neither made nor destroyed when things rot or burn. Antoine and Marie-Anne Lavoisier showed this by careful weighing in the 1780s.
Different plastics have different densities and do not mix well when melted, so they must be sorted before recycling.
Some bacteria and fungi have been found that can slowly break down certain plastics. Whether they could ever deal with the world's plastic is not known.

other_view.view: Waste is a problem of engineering, and using less is not the main answer. Sweden, Japan and Singapore handle their waste with sealed landfills, clean furnaces and good machines for sorting. Poor countries need those tools more than they need lessons about buying less. With good engineering, people can keep the benefits of cheap packaging and still have clean cities.

practice.title: Hold it before you throw it
practice.say: Before you throw the next thing out, hold it in both hands. Take one slow breath. Say what it is made of. Say how long you used it. Say where it will be tomorrow, and where it will be in a hundred years. Take one more slow breath. Then put it in the right bin.
practice.kid: Hold the thing in both hands. Breathe slowly once. Say what it is made of. Say how long you used it. Say where it will be in a hundred years. Breathe once more. Put it in the right bin.

playtest: Read through as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, step by step. The experiments, activities and games were reasoned through but have not been tried at home. The Float Tank Test (core) depends on two known facts: drink-bottle plastic is denser than water, and cap, milk-packet and takeaway-box plastics are less dense. Small flat pieces can rest on the surface or be held up by a bubble. So the steps add two drops of dish-washing liquid and push every piece under. The salt-water step shows something new only if a home has a solid thing marked 6. The step says so. Scrunch and Peel (core) needs an empty shelf carton. Its wall peels more easily after a soak. The silver layer may spring open a little, because plastic is stuck to it. The faint glow through a chips packet shows best in a dim room, on a part with little printing. The Crush Test needs four or five days of saved, rinsed dry waste. No step handles rotting waste. The Seven-Day Waste Count weighs closed bags and bins, with gloves and hand washing. Hazardous and sanitary waste is counted and never touched. A Dump That Does Not Leak uses fresh tea leaves as the 'waste'. The Last Landfill was played 4,000 times on a computer. With a good buying order the city wins nearly every game, with about 20 boxes ticked. With a poor order it wins fewer than half. Facts checked on 17 Nov 2026 against sources: the plastic figures (Geyer and others 2017), methane at 28 times (IPCC 2013), the British bag study, Love Canal dates, tonnage, families and law, the Deonar fire, the Ghazipur slide, Indore's cleanest-city ranking and bio-gas plant, Alappuzha in 2012, SWaCH since 2008, and the tin, aluminium and bottle lasting times.
